h1: About Pianoers.com
text: Hey. I'm Richard Abraham, the guy behind Pianoers . I started this site in 2021 because I was fed up with the same recycled garbage everywhere else. Glossy reviews for junk keyboards, "learn piano in 30 days" courses that leave you frustrated and broke, blogs that read like Amazon press releases. I wanted a place that just told the truth, even when the truth hurts. So that's exactly what Pianoers is. We buy the gear, we take the courses, we sit through every lesson, then we tell you what actually works and what sucks. No scripts, no fake smiles. If something is a scam, we call it. If a $200 keyboard outperforms a $2,000 console, we say that too. The team is small but legit: Richard Abraham – Founder and chief reviewer. Been obsessed with keys since I was 8, still gig on weekends, own too many pianos, and hate bad advice more than anything. Katarina – Lead teacher and adult-learner specialist. She has been teaching piano since 2001, holds a B.A. in Music from the University of Missouri, and has been a member of the National Association of Music Teachers since 1995. She knows exactly what busy adults need to get back into piano without wasting years on boring drills. Everything we publish is for real people who want real results fast: Adults restarting after years away Complete beginners who refuse to buy junk Parents who want their kid to actually stick with it Players ready to upgrade without getting ripped off We update constantly because new courses drop, prices change, and gear gets discontinued. We stay on it so you don't have to. If you've been looking for a no-BS piano site that actually cares about your progress, you're home. Welcome aboard. Richard & Katarina

h1: Cookie Policy
text: COOKIE POLICY Last updated May 16, 2024 This Cookie Policy explains how Pianoers.com (" Company ," " we ," " us ," and " our ") uses cookies and similar technologies to recognize you when you visit our website at https://pianoers.com (" Website "). It explains what these technologies are and why we use them, as well as your rights to control our use of them. In some cases we may use cookies to collect personal information, or that becomes personal information if we combine it with other information. What are cookies? Cookies are small data files that are placed on your computer or mobile device when you visit a website. Cookies are widely used by website owners in order to make their websites work, or to work more efficiently, as well as to provide reporting information. Cookies set by the website owner (in this case, Pianoers.com ) are called "first-party cookies." Cookies set by parties other than the website owner are called "third-party cookies." Third-party cookies enable third-party features or functionality to be provided on or through the website (e.g., advertising, interactive content, and analytics). The parties that set these third-party cookies can recognize your computer both when it visits the website in question and also when it visits certain other websites. Why do we use cookies? We use first- and third- party cookies for several reasons. Some cookies are required for technical reasons in order for our Website to operate, and we refer to these as "essential" or "strictly necessary" cookies. Other cookies also enable us to track and target the interests of our users to enhance the experience on our Online Properties. Third parties serve cookies through our Website for advertising, analytics, and other purposes. This is described in more detail below. How can I control cookies? You have the right to decide whether to accept or reject cookies. You can exercise your cookie rights by setting your preferences in the Cookie Consent Manager. The Cookie Consent Manager allows you to select which categories of cookies you accept or reject. Essential cookies cannot be rejected as they are strictly necessary to provide you with services. The Cookie Consent Manager can be found in the notification banner and on our website. If you choose to reject cookies, you may still use our website though your access to some functionality and areas of our website may be restricted. You may also set or amend your web browser controls to accept or refuse cookies. The specific types of first- and third-party cookies served through our Website and the purposes they perform are described in the table below (please note that the specific cookies served may vary depending on the specific Online Properties you visit): Analytics and customization cookies: These cookies collect information that is used either in aggregate form to help us understand how our Website is being used or how effective our marketing campaigns are, or to help us customize our Website for you. Persistent cookie that stays for 182 days Provider: .google.com Service: Google View Service Privacy Policy Type: server_cookie Expires in: 6 months Name: _ga Purpose: Records a particular ID used to come up with data about website usage by the user Provider: .pianoers.com Service: Google Analytics View Service Privacy Policy Type: http_cookie Expires in: 1 year 1 month 4 days Advertising cookies: These cookies are used to make advertising messages more relevant to you. They perform functions like preventing the same ad from continuously reappearing, ensuring that ads are properly displayed for advertisers, and in some cases selecting advertisements that are based on your interests. Name: _gcl_au Purpose: Used by Google AdSense for experimenting with advertisement efficiency across websites using their services. Provider: .pianoers.com Service: Google AdSense View Service Privacy Policy Type: http_cookie Expires in: 2 months 29 days Name: VISITOR_INFO1_LIVE Purpose: YouTube is a Google-owned platform for hosting and sharing videos. YouTube collects user data through videos embedded in websites, which is aggregated with profile data from other Google services in order to display targeted advertising to web visitors across a broad range of their own and other websites. Used by Google in combination with SID to verify Google user account and most recent login time. We are in the process of classifying these cookies with the help of their providers. As the means by which you can refuse cookies through your web browser controls vary from browser to browser, you should visit your browser's help menu for more information. The following is information about how to manage cookies on the most popular browsers: Chrome Internet Explorer Firefox Safari Edge Opera In addition, most advertising networks offer you a way to opt out of targeted advertising. If you would like to find out more information, please visit: Digital Advertising Alliance Digital Advertising Alliance of Canada European Interactive Digital Advertising Alliance What about other tracking technologies, like web beacons? Cookies are not the only way to recognize or track visitors to a website. We may use other, similar technologies from time to time, like web beacons (sometimes called "tracking pixels" or "clear gifs"). These are tiny graphics files that contain a unique identifier that enables us to recognize when someone has visited our Website or opened an email including them . This allows us, for example, to monitor the traffic patterns of users from one page within a website to another, to deliver or communicate with cookies, to understand whether you have come to the website from an online advertisement displayed on a third-party website, to improve site performance, and to measure the success of email marketing campaigns. In many instances, these technologies are reliant on cookies to function properly, and so declining cookies will impair their functioning. Do you use Flash cookies or Local Shared Objects? Websites may also use so-called "Flash Cookies" (also known as Local Shared Objects or "LSOs") to, among other things, collect and store information about your use of our services, fraud prevention, and for other site operations. If you do not want Flash Cookies stored on your computer, you can adjust the settings of your Flash player to block Flash Cookies storage using the tools contained in the Website Storage Settings Panel . You can also control Flash Cookies by going to the Global Storage Settings Panel and following the instructions (which may include instructions that explain, for example, how to delete existing Flash Cookies (referred to "information" on the Macromedia site), how to prevent Flash LSOs from being placed on your computer without your being asked, and (for Flash Player 8 and later) how to block Flash Cookies that are not being delivered by the operator of the page you are on at the time). Please note that setting the Flash Player to restrict or limit acceptance of Flash Cookies may reduce or impede the functionality of some Flash applications, including, potentially, Flash applications used in connection with our services or online content. Do you serve targeted advertising? Third parties may serve cookies on your computer or mobile device to serve advertising through our Website. These companies may use information about your visits to this and other websites in order to provide relevant advertisements about goods and services that you may be interested in. They may also employ technology that is used to measure the effectiveness of advertisements. They can accomplish this by using cookies or web beacons to collect information about your visits to this and other sites in order to provide relevant advertisements about goods and services of potential interest to you. The information collected through this process does not enable us or them to identify your name, contact details, or other details that directly identify you unless you choose to provide these. How often will you update this Cookie Policy? We may update this Cookie Policy from time to time in order to reflect, for example, changes to the cookies we use or for other operational, legal, or regulatory reasons. Please therefore revisit this Cookie Policy regularly to stay informed about our use of cookies and related technologies. The date at the top of this Cookie Policy indicates when it was last updated. Where can I get further information? If you have any questions about our use of cookies or other technologies, please email us at info@pianoers.com or by post to : Pianoers.com __________ __________

text: If you're starting piano right now and want something that actually feels good, sounds legit, and won't make you quit in three months… the Yamaha P-145 (or its Bluetooth sibling, the P-145BT ) is still sitting at the absolute top of my beginner recommendations in 2026 . I’ve had the original P-145 since it launched in 2023, hammered on it almost daily, lent it to students, moved it around apartments like it’s a laptop… and then in 2025 Yamaha released the P-145BT with the one upgrade everyone begged for. So yeah, I bought that one too. Spoiler: everything I’m about to say applies to both unless I call it out. P-145 vs P-145BT: What’s the Difference? Short answer: almost nothing except the feature that matters most to 90% of beginners. Model Bluetooth audio Everything else Price (Oct 2026) P-145 No (USB cable only) Identical Being phased out; Yamaha USA now lists only the BT P-145BT Yes: stream music from your phone Identical $499.99 list, often on sale That’s literally it. Same keys, same sound, same speakers, same weight. The BT version just lets you stream Spotify, YouTube or lesson audio straight through the piano’s speakers. It’s Bluetooth audio : the Smart Pianist app still connects with a USB cable (or Yamaha’s UD-BT01 wireless MIDI adaptor, sold separately). If you’re buying new today → just get the P-145BT and thank me later. Check the P-145BT price on Amazon How the P-145 Feels and Sounds Sit down and play one chord. Done. You’re sold. The Graded Hammer Compact (GHC) action is quieter than the old P-125/P-45, lighter than Roland/Casio competitors, but still properly graded (heavy in the bass, lighter up top). Fast repeats? Smooth and silent. No cheap clacking. I can practice at 1 a.m. without waking anyone, and it still teaches correct finger technique. Students who switch to an acoustic upright later barely notice the difference. Sound comes from Yamaha’s CFIIIS concert grand sample; bright, punchy, super clean. Not the absolute richest tone on the planet (Roland wins there), but easily the most “motivating” for beginners. Through headphones it’s stunning. Through the built-in 2×7W speakers it’s loud and clear enough for a bedroom or small apartment, way better than the downward-firing Rolands that get muffled on a desk. Yamaha P-145 Specs: What You Get 88 fully weighted GHC keys (quieter, smoother, lighter than most at this price) 64-note polyphony (plenty until you’re playing advanced Liszt) CFIIIS grand piano sound + 9 other usable voices Damper resonance, 4 reverb types, Duo mode (splits the keyboard into two identical halves for lessons) USB audio + MIDI interface (record straight into GarageBand or FL Studio with one cable) Smart Pianist and Rec’n’Share apps (over USB) Optional three-pedal unit (LP-5A) Weighs 24.5 lbs (11.1 kg): stupidly portable Runs on the included AC adaptor (no battery option) P-145BT only: Bluetooth audio (stream and play along wirelessly) Who the P-145 Is Best For Total beginners who want forgiving, quiet keys Adults returning to piano (no childish lights or 600 sounds) Tiny apartments / dorms / frequent movers Anyone who practices mostly with headphones or wants to jam over YouTube beats (P-145BT shines here) Downsides Speakers are good, not amazing. Fine unplugged, but you’ll eventually want headphones or external speakers for bigger rooms. 64-note polyphony is on the low side. Beginners never hit the limit, but heavy sustain-pedal classical players might, years down the line. No battery power, so it isn’t a busk-in-the-park keyboard. The original P-145 needs a cable for backing tracks. The P-145BT fixes that, but the app still wants a USB cable on both. Yamaha P-145 vs P-45 I owned and taught on the P-45 for years. Yamaha replaced it with the P-145 in 2023, so today you’ll mostly find it used or as leftover stock. Here’s the real difference: Quick Comparison Key Action P-145 / BT: GHC – quieter, smoother, lighter P-45: GHS – classic but clackier Winner: P-145 Key Noise P-145 / BT: Almost silent on fast repeats P-45: Noticeable thock-thock Winner: P-145 Sound P-145 / BT: Newer CFIIIS sample – brighter, richer P-45: Older sample – still great but flat Winner: P-145 Speakers P-145 / BT: 2×7W (clearer) P-45: 2×6W Winner: P-145 Connectivity P-145 / BT: USB audio + MIDI, Smart Pianist (BT adds Bluetooth audio) P-45: USB MIDI only Winner: P-145BT Size P-145 / BT: 10.6" deep, 24.5 lbs P-45: 11.5" deep, 25.3 lbs Winner: P-145 Price P-145BT: $499.99 list, often on sale P-45: Used or leftover stock only Winner: P-45 (if you find a deal) Bottom Line If you find a P-45 in great shape under $420 → buy it. Still fantastic. If the gap to the P-145BT is $50 or less → get the P-145BT. Quieter keys + Bluetooth audio are 100% worth it in 2026. I sold my P-45 the week the P-145 arrived. Enough said. My Verdict After Three Years (and Owning Both Versions) I’ve recommended the P-series to dozens of friends and students. Zero regrets. Zero returns. People text me months later saying they’re addicted. The P-145 was already the safe, no-drama king of beginner digital pianos. The P-145BT just removed the last tiny annoyance and made it basically perfect under $600. Demo of Yamaha P-145 (How it sounds) If you find a screaming deal on a leftover non-BT P-145 → still buy it. Otherwise? Get the P-145BT. You’ll use that Bluetooth every single day. Pair it with a good stand, bench, some closed-back headphones, and you’re set for the next 5–10 years easy. Way better than wasting money on a flashy 61-key toy you’ll outgrow in six months. Check the P-145BT price on Amazon Just get it. Then actually practice. That’s the part that matters way more than the gear. (Not sure how to start? Here are the online piano lessons I’d pick .) Still on the fence? Drop your budget, room size, or what you’re scared of in the comments and I’ll tell you straight if this is the one (or if something else snuck ahead while I wasn’t looking). Yamaha P-145 FAQ Is the Yamaha P-145 / P-145BT good for complete beginners? Yes. Hands down one of the best pianos for beginners you can buy right now. The keys are quiet, forgiving, and teach proper technique without fighting you. I’ve put total newbies on it and they’re still practicing months later instead of quitting. What’s the difference between the P-145 and P-145BT? Only Bluetooth audio. Everything else (keys, sound, speakers, weight) is identical. The BT version lets you stream backing tracks or YouTube lessons wirelessly through the piano’s speakers. The Smart Pianist app connects by USB cable on both. If you’re buying new, just get the P-145BT. Is the Yamaha P-145BT the best digital piano under $600 in 2026? For most beginners and budget-conscious adults, yes, still my #1. The Roland FP-10 is the closest rival, but the lighter, quieter Yamaha action + Bluetooth audio edges it out unless you specifically want a heavier “acoustic” feel. More options in my best digital pianos guide. Is the Yamaha P-145 still worth buying or is it discontinued? The original P-145 is being phased out: Yamaha USA now lists only the P-145BT, and new non-BT stock is drying up. If you find a leftover one at a good price, it’s the same piano minus Bluetooth. Otherwise grab the P-145BT. Zero regrets. Does the P-145 / P-145BT have weighted keys? Yes, 88 fully weighted, graded hammer keys (heavier in the bass, lighter in the treble) with the newer GHC mechanism. Feels way closer to a real piano than any “semi-weighted” or springy keyboard nonsense.

title: Piano Humidity and Temperature: Ideal Range and How to Hold It
desc: Keep a piano at 40 to 50% humidity and a steady 68 to 72°F. What dry and damp air do, why pitch drifts every season, and what to buy to keep it stable.
og_title: Piano Humidity and Temperature: Ideal Range and How to Hold It
og_desc: The ideal humidity and temperature for a piano, what happens outside that range, and the hygrometer, humidifier and placement habits that keep it stable all year.
author: Katarina
h1: Piano Humidity and Temperature: The Ideal Range and How to Hold It
headings: Why your piano goes out of tune every season
How to measure the humidity around your piano
Signs your piano has a humidity problem
What humidity should a piano be kept at?
What temperature is best for a piano?
Does cold weather damage a piano?
Why does my piano go out of tune every season?
Do I need a humidifier for my piano?
Can high humidity cause piano keys to stick?
Is a Dampp-Chaser system worth it?
How long should a piano settle after moving before tuning?
Do digital pianos need humidity control?
text: Keep your piano at 40 to 50 percent relative humidity and a steady room temperature around 68 to 72°F (20 to 22°C). Steinway's own guidance allows a wider band, 40 to 60 percent and 68 to 78°F, and the in-piano climate systems technicians install hold 42 percent. Every source agrees on the part that matters more than the number: keep the humidity steady. A piano that sits at 45 percent all year will outlast and out-tune one that swings from 30 percent in January to 65 percent in July. This guide covers what humidity and temperature do to a piano, how to measure them, and what to buy to keep them where they belong. Humidity at a glance Relative humidity What happens to the piano Below 30% Risk of soundboard cracks, loose tuning pins, failed glue joints 30 to 40% Pitch drifts flat, keys may click or feel loose 40 to 50% Ideal. Tuning and action stay stable 50 to 60% Pitch drifts sharp, action starts to feel heavy Above 60% Sticking keys, rusting strings and pins, risk of mold Why humidity matters so much Most of a piano is wood: the soundboard, the bridges, the pinblock that holds the tuning pins, the keys, and thousands of small action parts. Wood takes on moisture from humid air and gives it back to dry air, swelling and shrinking as it goes. Felt and cloth in the action do the same. A few percent of movement in a thin spruce soundboard or a felt bushing is enough to change how the piano sounds and plays. Repeated year after year, the same movement opens cracks and loosens joints. What high humidity does Above about 50 percent, the wood and felt swell. Keys stick or are slow to come back up. Swollen key bushings grip the guide pins, and the whole action feels heavy. The pitch goes sharp. The soundboard swells, pushes up on the bridges, and raises the tension on every string. Strings and tuning pins rust. Rusty strings sound dull and are more likely to break when a technician tunes them. Mold can grow on felts and inside the case if the room stays damp for weeks. What low humidity does Below about 40 percent, the wood dries and shrinks. The pitch goes flat. The soundboard loses its upward curve, called crown, and string tension drops. Tuning pins loosen. The pinblock shrinks around the pins, so the piano drifts out of tune faster and some pins stop holding at all. The soundboard can crack. Cracks often show up after a long, dry heating season. Keys click or wobble , and glue joints in the action and case can let go. Why your piano goes out of tune every season Seasonal tuning drift comes from humidity. Humid summer air swells the soundboard and the piano goes sharp. Once the heating comes on in winter and the air dries, the soundboard shrinks and the piano goes flat. Treble and bass don't move by the same amount, so the piano drifts out of tune with itself as well as off pitch. Temperature on its own moves the pitch far less. The reason a piano sounds worse in a cold, dry winter is the dry air, not the cold. This is also why the timing of a tuning matters. A piano tuned at the dry end of winter will be sharp by summer. Tuning once the season has settled, and holding the humidity steady, makes each tuning last. Temperature: steady beats exact Aim for a room that stays around 68 to 72°F, which is a comfortable room for people too. The danger is fast change rather than any particular temperature. Direct sunlight heats one side of the case, fades the finish, and dries the wood under it. Radiators, heating vents, air conditioning vents, and fireplaces blast hot or cold, dry air across the piano. Keep it well clear of all of them. Exterior walls and windows run colder in winter and warmer in summer than the room around them. Cold rooms are less of a problem than the moment they warm up. Warm, damp air hitting cold strings and plate can leave condensation, and condensation becomes rust. Warm an unheated room over several hours, not all at once. After a move, give the piano time to settle in its new room. Most technicians suggest waiting a couple of weeks before tuning, because the soundboard needs that long to adjust to the new humidity. How to measure the humidity around your piano You can't manage what you don't measure. A digital hygrometer costs less than a single tuning and tells you which problem you have. Put it near the piano , at about the height of the keys and away from vents and windows, so it reads the air the piano sits in. Check it weekly , and more often when the heating or air conditioning first comes on. Calibrate it once. Cheap hygrometers can read several points high or low. Seal it in a bag with a small dish of damp salt (salt with a few drops of water, not dissolved) for eight hours or so. The air in the bag settles at about 75 percent; the difference from your reading is the error to allow for. How to control humidity Most homes need help in one direction for part of the year and the other direction for the rest. There are two ways to give it. Control the room A humidifier for dry months. Choose a model with a built-in humidistat so it stops when the room reaches your target. Choose an evaporative humidifier where you can. Ultrasonic humidifiers filled with tap water throw out a fine white mineral dust that settles inside the piano; if you use one, fill it with distilled water. A dehumidifier for damp months , also with a humidistat, so it doesn't overdry the room. Air conditioning removes moisture as it cools, which helps in humid summers. Never point a humidifier, dehumidifier, or vent at the piano. Place the unit across the room and let the whole room reach the target. We cover choosing the equipment in more detail in our guides to piano humidifiers and piano dehumidifiers . Control the piano itself A Dampp-Chaser Piano Life Saver system goes inside the piano, fitted by a technician. It combines a humidistat, a humidifier with a water tank and wicking pads, and low-heat dehumidifier bars, and it holds the air inside the piano at about 42 percent all year. Cost: about $650 to $900 installed in an upright, $750 to $1,000 in a grand under 7 feet, and more in larger grands. Upkeep: add water when the warning light comes on, and replace the pads about once a year. Best for homes where the room can't be controlled: an older house with big seasonal swings, a church, a school, or a piano you can't move away from an exterior wall. It works best alongside sensible placement, not instead of it. Ask your technician whether your piano and your room justify one. Where to put your piano Against an interior wall, not an exterior one Out of direct sunlight at every time of day Well away from radiators, vents, and fireplaces Away from doors and windows that open to the outside Not in a basement, garage, conservatory, or bathroom-adjacent room, where humidity swings hardest A breathable cover keeps off dust and sun, but it does nothing for humidity, so don't rely on one. A seasonal routine Start of the heating season: check the hygrometer and start the humidifier as soon as the reading drops below 40 percent. Midwinter: check weekly. This is when cracks and loose pins start. Spring: turn the humidifier off as the air softens. Summer: run the dehumidifier or air conditioning if the reading climbs above 50 percent. Tuning: Steinway recommends two to four tunings a year for a piano played about an hour a day. Book them after each season has settled rather than at the start of a swing. Our guide to when your piano needs tuning covers the signs. Signs your piano has a humidity problem What you notice Likely cause Keys stick or are slow to come back up Humidity too high The piano sounds sharp, or tunings don't last through summer Humidity too high Rust on the strings or tuning pins Humidity too high, or condensation The piano sounds flat after winter Humidity too low Tuning pins turn with little resistance, or the piano won't hold a tuning Humidity too low, often for several winters Keys click or feel loose Humidity too low A buzz that wasn't there before Humidity too low: a soundboard crack or loose rib If you see the dry-air signs, raise the humidity a few points at a time rather than all at once, and book a technician to check the soundboard and pinblock. Frequently asked questions What humidity should a piano be kept at? Between 40 and 50 percent relative humidity, with 45 percent a good target. Steinway allows 40 to 60 percent, and in-piano climate systems hold 42 percent. Keeping the level steady matters more than hitting an exact number. What temperature is best for a piano? A steady room temperature of about 68 to 72°F (20 to 22°C). Steinway's guidance allows 68 to 78°F. Avoid fast changes, direct sunlight, and heating or cooling vents. Does cold weather damage a piano? Cold by itself does little harm. The risks come from the dry air that winter heating creates, and from warming a cold piano too fast, which can leave condensation on the strings. Warm a cold room over several hours. Why does my piano go out of tune every season? Because the humidity changes. Humid summer air swells the soundboard and pushes the pitch sharp; dry winter air shrinks it and pulls the pitch flat. Steady humidity makes tunings last longer. Do I need a humidifier for my piano? If your hygrometer reads below 40 percent for weeks at a time, which in most homes means the heating season, yes. Use a room humidifier with a humidistat, evaporative if possible, placed away from the piano. Can high humidity cause piano keys to stick? Yes. Above about 50 percent, the wooden keys and the felt bushings around their guide pins swell, so keys stick or are slow to come back up. Bringing the humidity down frees most of them within days. Is a Dampp-Chaser system worth it? It's worth it in rooms you can't control, such as old houses with big seasonal swings, churches, and schools. It holds the inside of the piano at about 42 percent and costs about $650 to $1,000 installed. In a well-controlled room, a hygrometer and a room humidifier do the same job for less. How long should a piano settle after moving before tuning? Most technicians suggest a couple of weeks, so the soundboard can adjust to the humidity in its new room. A tuning done straight after a move tends to drift. Do digital pianos need humidity control? Not in the same way. Digital pianos have no soundboard or strings, so humidity doesn't change their pitch or tuning. Keep them away from damp, direct sun, and heat sources to protect the electronics, as you would any electrical equipment. The short version Buy a hygrometer, keep the reading between 40 and 50 percent, and keep it there all year. Put the piano on an interior wall away from sun, vents, and heaters. Humidify in winter, dehumidify in summer, and time your tunings for when each season has settled. Those habits prevent almost every climate problem a piano can have, and they cost far less than repairing a cracked soundboard.

Or worse, which one will make me quit in a month because it feels like tapping on cardboard? I've been there. I've tested tons of beginner-friendly digital pianos over the years (and yeah, I've got opinions). Whether you're a total newbie or just getting back into it, here's a deep dive into the best beginner pianos that are actually fun to play, and won't kill your budget. Quick note on wording: lots of people search for a "beginner keyboard piano," but what a beginner really wants is a digital piano, meaning a keyboard with 88 fully weighted keys. Every pick below is one. Heads-up: some links on this page are Amazon affiliate links. If you buy through one, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. It never decides which pianos make this list. Quick answer The best beginner keyboard piano for most people is the Yamaha P-145BT It costs about $500 and has fully weighted keys, a clean piano tone and Bluetooth audio. On a tight budget, get the Alesis Recital Pro (about $400). If key feel matters most, the Roland FP-10 (about $499) has the same PHA-4 action as Roland's pricier FP-30X. For the best sound around $500, pick the Kawai ES60 . Semi-weighted or unweighted keys will teach your fingers all the wrong habits. If you want to develop real technique and eventually play an acoustic piano, you need fully weighted, hammer-action keys. No exceptions. From $500 to $750 you're paying for extras like Bluetooth audio and better speakers (great if you can swing it, but not necessary to start). Spending more than that? See my best digital pianos guide. App connectivity makes practice more fun. Being able to connect your piano to learning apps like Simply Piano , Flowkey , or GarageBand keeps you coming back to the keys. Weighted keys that give you feedback without being stiff, clean piano tone, and a layout that doesn't try to impress you with a billion flashing buttons. It's like Yamaha knew exactly what you needed and nothing more. The P-145 has been my go-to recommendation for over a year now, and Yamaha just made it even better by releasing the P-145BT with built-in Bluetooth audio. Same exact piano, same keys, same sound, but now you can wirelessly stream Spotify, YouTube lessons, or backing tracks straight through the piano's speakers. For about $50 more than the original, it's a no-brainer upgrade. If you want the full breakdown, read my Yamaha P-145 / P-145BT review . Downsides? The speakers are just okay. Nothing spectacular. And 64-note polyphony is the lowest on this list, though beginners will never notice the limit. The original P-145 (without Bluetooth) is getting harder to find new, so go for the BT version. My Take: If you want to learn piano and you're not interested in shiny gimmicks, this is your jam. It's durable, portable, and feels like a real instrument. The BT version fixes the only thing the original was missing. 2 Best on a budget Alesis Recital Pro “The best cheap digital piano that doesn't feel like a toy.” Verdict: The Alesis Recital Pro is the cheapest digital piano I'd recommend to a beginner: 88 hammer-action keys and 128-note polyphony for about $400, with a less refined feel than Yamaha or Roland. What It Has: 88 full-sized hammer-action keys 12 voices (including organ, synth, etc.) Lesson mode, split mode, and layer mode 128-note polyphony Built-in speakers and headphone output USB-MIDI for app connectivity 26 lbs Best For: Absolute beginners on a tight budget, parents buying a first piano for their kids, or someone testing the waters before committing. Check price on Amazon Street price about $450–$550, checked Oct 6, 2026 Action RHL graded Polyphony 192 Bluetooth No Weight 24 lbs Why it's here Shigeru Kawai SK-EX concert grand samples 192-note polyphony Stereo line outputs, rare at this price Watch out for No Bluetooth, so apps need a cable No built-in recorder Why I Recommend It: The ES60 is the most affordable model in Kawai's ES series, and it might be the best-sounding beginner piano you can buy right now. The secret is the sound source: it uses samples from the Shigeru Kawai SK-EX, a handmade concert grand that professional pianists perform on in recital halls around the world. You're hearing that piano through an instrument that sells for about $450–$550 (list price $599). It's kind of absurd. The new Responsive Hammer Lite (RHL) action is smooth and comfortable with a nice graded feel. It's lighter than Roland's PHA-4, which some people will prefer and others won't. At just 24 lbs, it's also one of the most portable options on this list. What It Has: 88 keys with Responsive Hammer Lite (RHL) graded action Shigeru Kawai SK-EX concert grand piano samples Harmonic Imaging sound engine 17 instrument voices 192-note polyphony Dual and Split playing modes 30 built-in drum rhythms USB-MIDI for app connectivity (works with Kawai PianoRemote app) Dedicated stereo line outputs (rare at this price) Built-in speakers (10W + 10W) 24 lbs Best For: Beginners who prioritize sound quality above everything else. Also great for anyone who wants to buy into the Kawai ecosystem at an affordable price. Downsides? No Bluetooth, so you'll need a wired connection for apps. The key action, while good, isn't as proven as Yamaha's GHC or Roland's PHA-4. And there's no built-in recording feature. My Take: If piano tone is what makes you want to keep playing, the ES60 might be your best motivator. Kawai's been making pianos since 1927, and you can genuinely hear that heritage in every note. It's a stunning debut at this price. 4 Best key feel Roland FP-10 “Entry-level price, but definitely not entry-level keys.” Verdict: The Roland FP-10 gives you the best key feel under $500, with the same PHA-4 Standard action as the FP-30X, in exchange for fewer sounds and small speakers. Check price on Amazon Street price about $499, checked Oct 6, 2026 Action PHA-4 Standard Polyphony 96 Bluetooth MIDI only Weight 28 lbs Why it's here Same keys as Roland's pricier FP-30X SuperNATURAL piano tone Bluetooth MIDI for learning apps Watch out for Only 15 sounds on the panel No Bluetooth audio, small speakers Why I Recommend It: The FP-10 is Roland's cheapest 88-key digital piano, but here's the thing: it shares the exact same PHA-4 Standard key action as the more expensive FP-30X (which costs about $150 more). You're getting Roland's signature key feel at a fraction of the price. The trade-off? Fewer sounds, no Bluetooth audio, simpler speakers. But the keys (the most important part) are the real deal. Roland's SuperNATURAL sound engine is in here too, giving you a clean and dynamic piano tone that responds beautifully to how hard or soft you play. What It Has: 88 keys with PHA-4 Standard action Roland SuperNATURAL sound engine 15 tones (36 in total) 96-note polyphony Bluetooth MIDI (works with the Roland Piano App) USB to Host Built-in speakers (6W + 6W) 28 lbs Best For: Complete beginners who want the best feeling keys they can get under $500. Also a solid choice for parents buying a first piano. Downsides? Very basic feature set: only 15 sounds, no Bluetooth audio, and the speakers are small. My Take: If key feel is your top priority and you don't care about extras, the FP-10 punches way above its weight. The PHA-4 action is genuinely impressive at any price, let alone under $500. 5 Simplest Korg B2 “Underrated. Super beginner-friendly and sounds better than expected.” Verdict: The Korg B2 is the simplest piano on this list, with warm German and Italian grand samples and bundled lesson software, but stock is getting hard to find. Sold out at Korg's US store; the B2+ replaces it Check price on Amazon Street price about $500, checked Oct 6, 2026 Action NH weighted Polyphony 120 Bluetooth No Weight 25 lbs Why it's here Warm German and Italian grand pianos USB audio and MIDI Very simple to use Watch out for Pedal jack only takes Korg pedals No Bluetooth Why I Recommend It: Korg doesn't get as much love in the beginner space, but the B2 is a dark horse. It's simple, affordable, and sounds surprisingly warm. The German and Italian grand piano samples are beautiful for the price, and the Natural Weighted Hammer action provides a decent feel. Plus, it has USB connectivity to hook up learning apps like Flowkey or Simply Piano, and comes with a three-month Skoove trial. What It Has: 88 keys with NH (Natural Weighted Hammer) action 12 built-in sounds (5 pianos, plus electric piano, organ, strings, harpsichord) 120-note polyphony USB Audio and MIDI Built-in speakers (15W + 15W) Includes a 3-month Skoove trial plus the KORG Module and KORG Gadget 2 Le apps 25 lbs Best For: Beginners who want something basic, reliable, and musical without overcomplicating things. Downsides? No Bluetooth. The proprietary pedal connector is frustrating (you can't use third-party pedals). And a heads-up: Korg's own US store now lists the B2 as sold out, and the newer B2+ (about $600 on sale) has taken its place, so availability is limited.  Check stock before you fall in love with it. My Take: Still a solid piano if you can find one at a good price. But with the Kawai ES60 selling for about $450–$550, the B2 faces stiff competition. If you're choosing between the two, the ES60 sounds better and has more polyphony. 6 Best for growth Roland FP-30X “Fancy, but not flashy. A future-proof pick if you're in it for the long haul.” Verdict: The Roland FP-30X is the best buy-once beginner piano if you can spend about $650–$700: the same PHA-4 keys as the FP-10, plus Bluetooth audio and MIDI, 256-note polyphony and bigger speakers. Check price on Amazon Street price about $650–$700, checked Oct 6, 2026 Action PHA-4 Standard Polyphony 256 Bluetooth Audio + MIDI Weight 33 lbs Why it's here Bluetooth audio and MIDI 256-note polyphony, 56 sounds Bigger 11 W speakers Watch out for About $250 more than the cheapest pick Button combinations for most settings Why I Recommend It: The FP-30X is technically priced above the beginner range at around $650–$700, but I'm including it because it's the single best "buy once, don't upgrade for years" piano you can get. It uses the same PHA-4 Standard action as the FP-10 (escapement, Ivory Feel keytops), so you're not paying extra for better keys. You're paying for everything around them: Bluetooth audio, 256-note polyphony, 56 voices and much bigger speakers. That escapement, by the way, is the subtle "click" you feel when you press a key. It mimics what happens inside a grand piano. And then there's Bluetooth. MIDI and audio. Wirelessly stream your favorite songs through the piano's speakers while you play along. Connect to Simply Piano or Flowkey without a single cable. What It Has: 88 keys with PHA-4 Standard action (escapement + Ivory Feel keytops) Roland SuperNATURAL sound engine 56 instrument voices 256-note polyphony Bluetooth audio + Bluetooth MIDI Built-in recorder and metronome Built-in speakers (11W + 11W) 33 lbs Best For: Intermediate beginners, adult learners, or tech-savvy players who want to grow into their instrument and not replace it in two years. Downsides? At $650–$700, it costs about $250 more than the cheapest option on this list. It's also 33 lbs, so portability takes a small hit. And the user interface (button combinations for everything) is clunky. My Take: If you can stretch your budget past $500, this is where the magic starts. The feel is genuinely impressive, and the Bluetooth audio alone makes practice sessions so much more fun. This piano grows with you. It's the one I recommend when someone says "I'm serious about this." 7 Best for small spaces Casio Privia PX-S1100 “Sleek and slim, but still plays like a beast.” Verdict: The Casio Privia PX-S1100 is the best beginner piano for small spaces: one of the slimmest 88-key weighted pianos you can buy, with Bluetooth audio and MIDI, for about $730. Check price on Amazon Street price about $730, checked Oct 6, 2026 Action Smart Scaled Hammer Polyphony 192 Bluetooth Audio + MIDI (adapter) Depth 9.1 in Why it's here About 9 inches deep and 25 lbs Bluetooth via the included adapter Black, white or red Watch out for Priced alongside the FP-30X Touch controls take getting used to Why I Recommend It: At around $730, the PX-S1100 isn't exactly a budget pick anymore. But I'm including it because nothing else on this list looks or feels quite like it. Casio knocked it out of the park here. This thing looks like it belongs in a design museum, but plays like a serious instrument. It's super slim (about 9 inches deep), yet the keys still have real hammer action. The piano tone is expressive, powered by Casio's Multi-Dimensional Morphing AiR sound engine, and the included Bluetooth adapter adds wireless audio and MIDI for playing along with your favorite songs. What It Has: 88 fully-weighted keys (Smart Scaled Hammer Action) Multi-Dimensional Morphing AiR sound engine 18 instrument voices 192-note polyphony Bluetooth audio and MIDI (via the included WU-BT10 adapter) USB-MIDI Stylish design, available in black, white, or red 25 lbs Best For: People with limited space, style-conscious players, and anyone who wants something portable and beautiful. Downsides? At ~$730, it's priced alongside the FP-30X, which has better key action. Touch-sensitive controls instead of buttons take some getting used to. And the key action, while decent, doesn't feel quite as refined as the Roland PHA-4 or Kawai RHL in terms of realism. My Take: If looks matter and you don't want to sacrifice feel or sound, this is a fantastic choice. Perfect for apartment living. The Bluetooth audio is a nice bonus for practice sessions. Just Want a Keyboard to Try? (Kids and Tight Budgets) Everything above has 88 weighted keys, because that's what you need to learn piano properly. But if you're buying for a young child, or you just want to find out whether you enjoy playing before spending $400 or more, a light portable keyboard is a reasonable first step. Plan to move up to one of the pianos above once lessons get serious. Casio Casiotone CT-S1 (about $220–$260): 61 full-size, touch-sensitive keys (not weighted), runs on six AA batteries, and weighs about 10 lbs. Yamaha NP-15 (about $270): 61 touch-sensitive keys, 15 voices and a slim 11.5-lb body that also runs on batteries. Korg Liano (about $400): all 88 keys in a 13-lb body that runs up to 8 hours on batteries, but the keys are light-touch, not weighted, so treat it as a stepping stone, not a practice piano. For very young kids, also read our Loog Piano review . Bonus: Don't Ignore These Tips 1. Headphone jack = peace. Seriously. Practice without bugging the whole house. Every piano on this list has one. 2. Buy a stand and pedal. A proper stand (not an X-stand) and a sustain pedal will make your setup way more comfortable and realistic. Most of these pianos come with a basic pedal, but upgrading to a proper one later makes a real difference. 3. Try before you buy (if possible). Key action is a deeply personal thing. What feels perfect to me might feel too heavy or too light for you. Hit up a Guitar Center or local music store and play a few models. If you can't, buy from a retailer with a good return policy. 4. Don't sleep on learning apps. Pairing your piano with an app like Flowkey, Simply Piano, or Pianoforall makes the first few months so much more enjoyable. If your piano has Bluetooth MIDI or USB, you're set. Check out our best free piano learning apps for more options. 5. Avoid no-name brands. Those suspiciously cheap "88-key weighted pianos" from unknown brands on Amazon? They cut corners on key action and sound quality. You'll notice within a week, and you'll want to upgrade within a month. Stick to Yamaha, Roland, Kawai, Casio, Korg, or Alesis. Frequently Asked Questions How much should a beginner spend on a digital piano? $400 to $500 covers most beginners. That gets you fully weighted keys and a good piano sound. Under $400 you start compromising on key feel, and the Alesis Recital Pro is about as low as I'd go. If you can stretch to around $700, the Roland FP-30X adds Bluetooth audio, better speakers and more voices on the same keys as the Roland FP-10. Do I need 88 keys as a beginner? Strongly recommended, yes. Most piano music uses the full range, and even if you don't need all 88 keys right away, you'll grow into them fast. Starting on a 61-key keyboard can build habits that are hard to break later. What's the difference between a keyboard and a digital piano? A keyboard usually has unweighted or semi-weighted keys and focuses on having lots of sounds and rhythms. A digital piano focuses on replicating the feel and sound of a real acoustic piano with fully weighted keys. If your goal is to learn piano , get a digital piano. For a deeper dive, check out our piano basics guide . Can I learn piano on a digital piano instead of an acoustic? Absolutely. Digital pianos are actually better for learning in many ways. You can practice with headphones at any hour, connect to learning apps , record yourself, and use the built-in metronome. Most piano teachers are perfectly happy with students practicing on a quality digital piano. We break this down fully in our acoustic vs digital piano comparison. Are weighted keys really that important for beginners? Yes. 100%. Weighted keys build proper finger strength and technique from day one. If you practice on unweighted keys, your fingers won't develop the control needed for an acoustic piano. It's like training for a marathon in slippers. Which brand makes the best beginner digital piano? They're all good at different things. Yamaha is the safest all-rounder. Roland has the best key feel for the money. Kawai has the best sound quality. Casio has the best design and portability. You really can't go wrong with any of them. Is a 61-key keyboard OK for a child? For a young child or a just-curious beginner, a light 61-key keyboard like the Casio CT-S1 is fine for the first few months. Once lessons get serious, move to an 88-key digital piano with weighted keys, because unweighted keys don't build the finger control an acoustic piano needs. Still Not Sure? Here's My TL;DR If you're still stuck, here's my advice: don't overthink it. Pick one in your budget and just start playing. Best all-around: Yamaha P-145BT Tightest budget: Alesis Recital Pro Best sound: Kawai ES60 Best key feel: Roland FP-10 Simplest: Korg B2 Worth the splurge: Roland FP-30X Smallest space: Casio PX-S1100 The real magic is in practice, not gear. Send me a message if you want help picking one based on your space, goals, or learning style. Happy to help. Just promise me one thing: Stick with it. Because piano is one of the most rewarding things you'll ever learn. And if you're just getting started, check out our articles on the best online piano lessons and how to teach yourself piano .
