text: So you've decided you want a digital piano. Smart move. But now you're drowning in model numbers (CLP-this, FP-that, PX-whatever) and every website is telling you something different. One says Yamaha is king. Another says Roland. Someone on Reddit swears by Kawai. And there's always that guy recommending a $200 Amazon keyboard that'll "totally work fine." Spoiler: it won't. I've spent the last few years obsessively testing, comparing, and playing digital pianos at every price point. From $400 slab-style portables to $4,000+ furniture-style consoles that look like they belong in a movie set. And I've got opinions. Whether you're a total beginner looking for your first real instrument, an intermediate player ready to level up, or someone who just wants the best damn piano they can fit in their apartment, this guide has you covered. Here's every digital piano I'd actually recommend in 2026, organized by budget so you can skip straight to what matters to you . My Top Picks at a Glance The best digital piano picks split cleanly by budget and goal: Yamaha P-145BT for most beginners, Roland FP-10 for best key action under $600, and Kawai ES60 for tone. For intermediate players, the Yamaha P-225 and Roland FP-30X deliver stronger speakers, better actions, and longer-term value. Best Overall (Beginner): Yamaha P-145BT Best Budget Beginner: Roland FP-10 Best Beginner Sound: Kawai ES60 Best for Growth: Roland FP-30X Best Slim & Stylish: Casio PX-S1100 Best Intermediate Portable: Kawai ES920 Best for Gigging: Casio PX-S3100 Best Budget Console: Kawai KDP120 Best Mid-Range Console: Yamaha CLP-835 Best Premium Console: Yamaha CLP-885 Best High-End Portable: Roland FP-90X Best Digital Pianos for Beginners (Under $500) Starting out? You don't need to spend a fortune, but you do need weighted keys. That's non-negotiable. Semi-weighted or unweighted keys will teach your fingers all the wrong habits, and switching to a real piano later will feel like moving from a tricycle to a motorcycle. Here are my picks for beginners who want something that actually feels like a piano. 1. Yamaha P-145BT — Best Beginner Digital Piano 💬 "The one I recommend more than any other piano. Period." Yamaha P-145BT Why I Recommend It: You already know I love this one if you've read my full Yamaha P-145 review . It's simple, reliable, and plays like an instrument that costs twice as much. The Graded Hammer Compact action feels natural under your fingers: heavier on the left, lighter on the right, just like a real piano. The tone is clean and warm, sampled from Yamaha's legendary CFX concert grand. No gimmicks, no fuss, just a solid piano that lets you focus on actually playing . Current Best Deal on Amazon What It Has: 88 fully weighted keys (GHC action) Yamaha CFX-sampled piano voice 24 instrument voices USB to Host for app connectivity Built-in speakers (7W + 7W) Super lightweight at just 24 lbs Best For: Anyone who wants a no-nonsense practice piano that feels close to the real thing. Downsides? The onboard speakers are just okay. Nothing spectacular. And the feature set is minimal. But honestly? For a beginner, fewer distractions is a good thing. My Take: If someone asks me "what digital piano should I buy?" and they're a beginner, I say Yamaha P-145BT without even thinking about it. It's the safest, smartest first piano you can get. Pair it with headphones and a decent stand, and you're set for at least a couple of years. 2. Roland FP-10 — Best Budget Beginner 💬 "Entry-level, but doesn't play like it." Roland FP-10 Why I Recommend It: The FP-10 is Roland's cheapest 88-key digital piano, but here's the thing: it shares the exact same PHA-4 Standard key action as the more expensive FP-30X (which costs $200 more). Let that sink in. You're getting Roland's signature key feel at a fraction of the price. The trade-off? Fewer sounds, no Bluetooth audio, simpler speakers. But the keys (the most important part) are the real deal. Roland's SuperNATURAL sound engine is in here too, giving you a clean and dynamic piano tone that responds beautifully to how hard or soft you play. Current Best Deal on Amazon What It Has: 88 keys with PHA-4 Standard action Roland SuperNATURAL sound engine 15 tones 96-note polyphony Bluetooth MIDI (via Roland Piano Partner app) USB to Host Built-in speakers (6W + 6W) Best For: Complete beginners who want real key feel without breaking the bank. Also a solid choice for parents buying a first piano. Downsides? Very basic feature set: only 15 sounds, no Bluetooth audio, and the speakers are small. No headphone 3D ambience like the FP-30X. My Take: If your budget is tight and you want the best feeling piano you can get under $500, the FP-10 is hard to beat. It punches way above its weight where it matters most. 3. Kawai ES60 — Best Beginner Piano Sound 💬 "The new kid on the block that sounds like a $250,000 concert grand." Kawai ES60 Why I Recommend It: Kawai finally entered the under-$500 game, and they didn't mess around. The ES60 uses samples from the Shigeru Kawai SK-EX, a handmade concert grand that sits alongside Steinways and Bösendorfers in the world's best recital halls. You're getting that sound in a $499 piano. The new Responsive Hammer Lite (RHL) action is on the lighter side compared to Roland's PHA-4, but it's smooth, comfortable, and beautifully graded. And at just 24 lbs, it's one of the lightest 88-key weighted pianos on the market. Throw it in a gig bag and go. Current Best Deal on Amazon What It Has: 88 keys with Responsive Hammer Lite (RHL) action Shigeru Kawai SK-EX concert grand piano samples Harmonic Imaging sound engine 17 instrument voices 192-note polyphony (massive for this price) Dual and Split playing modes 30 built-in drum rhythms USB-MIDI for app connectivity Dedicated stereo line outputs Built-in speakers (10W + 10W) Best For: Beginners who prioritize sound quality above everything else. Also great for anyone who wants Kawai quality at a beginner price. Downsides? No Bluetooth, so you'll need a wired connection for apps. The key action, while good, isn't as consistent as the FP-10's PHA-4 or as established as the P-145's GHC. And no recording feature built in. My Take: If piano tone is what matters most to you, the ES60 might be the best-sounding beginner piano you can buy right now. That SK-EX sample set is genuinely stunning for this price point. Kawai's been making pianos since 1927, and you can hear it. Best Intermediate Digital Pianos ($700–$2,000) Intermediate digital pianos are models with better key action, stronger amplification, and more expressive sound than entry-level boards, typically priced from $700 to $2,000. Standout options include the Yamaha P-225, Roland FP-30X, and Kawai ES120, which add graded hammer actions, improved speakers, and Bluetooth or app support. This is the sweet spot of digital pianos. Not insanely expensive, but good enough that even classically trained pianists won't scoff at them. 1. Roland FP-30X — Best for Long-Term Growth 💬 "The one you buy once and don't upgrade for years." Roland FP-30X Why I Recommend It: I covered this in my beginner pianos article too, and it still holds up. At around $695, the FP-30X sits right at the border between beginner and intermediate, which makes it a brilliant choice for anyone who's serious about sticking with piano. The PHA-4 Standard key action with escapement and Ivory Feel keytops is a massive step up from cheaper models. You actually feel a subtle "click" when you press the keys. That's the escapement mechanism mimicking what happens inside a grand piano. And then there's Bluetooth. MIDI and audio. Wirelessly stream your favorite songs through the piano's speakers while you play along. Connect to Simply Piano or Flowkey without a single cable. This is the future, and it's pretty sweet. Current Best Deal on Amazon What It Has: 88 keys with PHA-4 Standard action (escapement + Ivory Feel) Roland SuperNATURAL sound engine Bluetooth MIDI + Bluetooth audio 256-note polyphony 56 instrument voices Built-in recorder and metronome Headphone 3D ambience Best For: Adult learners, intermediate beginners, or anyone who wants one piano that'll last them for years without needing an upgrade. Downsides? At $695–$700, it's a step up from the true beginner tier. It's also heavier than the P-145 or FP-10, so if portability matters, keep that in mind. My Take: If you can stretch your budget past $500, this is where the magic starts. The feel is genuinely impressive for this price range, and the Bluetooth audio alone makes practice sessions so much more fun. This piano grows with you. 2. Casio Privia PX-S1100 — Best Slim & Stylish 💬 "Looks like a design object. Plays like a proper instrument." Casio Privia PX-S1100 Why I Recommend It: I mentioned this in my beginner pianos piece too, and it's still one of my favorites. The PX-S1100 is absurdly slim. We're talking world's thinnest digital piano territory. But don't let the sleek looks fool you. It has Casio's Smart Scaled Hammer Action, which provides a surprisingly realistic feel for something this compact. The piano tone is built on Casio's Multi-Dimensional Morphing AiR sound source, and it sounds genuinely good. Clean highs, warm lows, and decent dynamic range. Plus, Bluetooth audio lets you stream music through the piano's speakers, perfect for playing along with your favorite tracks. Current Best Deal on Amazon What It Has: 88 fully weighted keys (Smart Scaled Hammer Action) Multi-Dimensional Morphing AiR sound engine 18 voices 192-note polyphony Bluetooth audio USB-MIDI Available in black, white, or red Incredibly slim and light (25 lbs) Best For: Apartment dwellers, style-conscious players, anyone who needs a quality piano that won't dominate their living space. Downsides? The touch-sensitive controls (instead of physical buttons) take some getting used to. You'll accidentally change settings while cleaning the thing. And the key action, while good, isn't in the same league as the Roland or Kawai models at this price. My Take: If your space is limited or aesthetics matter to you (no judgment, they matter to me too), the PX-S1100 is a fantastic choice. It proves that a piano can be beautiful and functional. 3. Kawai ES920 — Best Intermediate Portable 💬 "The sleeper hit. Most people don't know about Kawai, and that's their loss." Kawai ES920 Why I Recommend It: Kawai is the brand that doesn't get enough love in the beginner space, but among intermediate and advanced players? They're royalty. The ES920 has Kawai's Responsive Hammer III action with 88 keys with triple-sensor detection, counterweights, and let-off simulation. Translation: it feels incredible . The sound engine uses Harmonic Imaging XL technology, built from samples of Kawai's flagship SK-EX concert grand. It's rich, expressive, and responds to your touch in a way that cheaper pianos simply can't. Current Best Deal on Amazon What It Has: 88 keys with RH III action (triple sensor, counterweights, let-off) Harmonic Imaging XL sound engine (SK-EX samples) 256-note polyphony Bluetooth MIDI + audio 38 instrument voices Line out, USB, MIDI Onboard recorder Powerful speakers (20W + 20W) Best For: Intermediate players who want professional-grade key action and sound in a portable package. Also great for gigging musicians. Downsides? It's not cheap, typically around $1,950. And it doesn't have the brand recognition of Yamaha or Roland, so finding demos in local stores can be harder. My Take: If you're past the beginner phase and want a portable piano that can truly rival the feel of an acoustic, the ES920 is the one to get. I was genuinely surprised the first time I played it. The action is buttery smooth and the sound has real depth. 4. Casio PX-S3100 — Best for Gigging & Versatility 💬 "It's a piano. It's a workstation. It's ridiculously portable." Casio PX-S3100 Why I Recommend It: While the PX-S1100 keeps things focused on piano, the PX-S3100 opens the floodgates. You get the same slim body and hammer action, but now with 700+ tones, 200 rhythms, a pitch bend wheel, and knobs for real-time sound control. If you're a gigging musician, a songwriter, or someone who likes to experiment beyond just piano, this is your Swiss Army knife. And it still weighs about 24 lbs. That's insane for what it packs in. Current Best Deal on Amazon What It Has: 88 fully weighted keys (Smart Scaled Hammer Action) 700+ tones (including synths, organs, strings, and more) 200 built-in rhythms with auto-accompaniment Pitch bend wheel and 2 assignable knobs Bluetooth MIDI + audio Mic input with vocal effects USB audio recording Battery operation option Best For: Gigging musicians, singer-songwriters, producers, or anyone who wants a versatile music workstation that also happens to be a solid piano. Downsides? The piano purists will argue (correctly) that the key action isn't as refined as Kawai or Roland models at this price. And with 700+ sounds, the interface can feel overwhelming at first. My Take: This isn't just a digital piano. It's a creative tool. If you only play classical piano, you don't need this. But if you like to mess around with sounds, play gigs, or produce music? The PX-S3100 is ridiculously fun and absurdly portable. Best Console (Home) Digital Pianos Console pianos are the ones that look like actual furniture. They've got built-in stands, proper three-pedal units, and (this is the big one) significantly better speaker systems than portable models. If your piano is staying in one spot at home, a console is almost always the better choice. Yeah, they cost more. But you're paying for an experience that's genuinely closer to sitting at an acoustic piano. 1. Kawai KDP120 — Best Budget Console 💬 "The affordable console that doesn't cut corners where it counts." Kawai KDP120 Why I Recommend It: If you want a proper furniture-style piano without spending $2,000+, the KDP120 is your answer. Kawai packed their Responsive Hammer Compact II action in here. It's not as advanced as the RH III in the ES920, but it's still a very satisfying key action with a realistic weight gradient. The sound comes from Kawai's Harmonic Imaging engine with 15 instrument voices, and the two 20W speakers in the cabinet produce a much fuller sound than any portable piano in this price range. It also comes with a matching bench in some bundles, which is a nice touch. Current Best Deal on Amazon What It Has: 88 keys with RH Compact II action Harmonic Imaging sound engine 15 instrument voices 192-note polyphony Built-in 3-pedal unit Elegant furniture cabinet Headphone jacks x 2 USB to Host Best For: Beginners and intermediate players who want a console piano experience without the premium price tag. Downsides? No Bluetooth. The feature set is intentionally minimal: no recorder, no split/layer modes, no fancy connectivity. And the sound, while good, doesn't have the complexity of the CLP-835 or CN301. My Take: The KDP120 is proof that you don't need to spend a fortune to get a beautiful-looking, great-sounding home piano. If you're on a budget and want something that'll look elegant in your living room, this is it. 2. Yamaha CLP-835 — Best Mid-Range Console 💬 "This is where digital starts feeling like acoustic." Yamaha CLP-835 Why I Recommend It: The CLP-835 is part of Yamaha's legendary Clavinova line, and honestly? This is where things get really good. The GrandTouch-S keyboard has long, wooden keys that move and feel remarkably close to a concert grand. Yamaha's CFX and Bösendorfer Imperial voices are both included, two of the world's most iconic grand piano sounds, captured with obsessive detail. But what truly sets the CLP-835 apart is the technology working behind the scenes. Virtual Resonance Modeling (VRM) recreates how strings interact inside a real piano. When you hold down one note and play another, you hear subtle overtones and sympathetic vibrations. Grand Expression Modeling captures how your touch changes the sound, not just how hard you press but how you release, how you transition between notes. It's subtle stuff, but it's the kind of thing that makes you go "whoa, this actually feels alive." Current Best Deal on Yamaha What It Has: 88 keys with GrandTouch-S action (wooden keys) Yamaha CFX and Bösendorfer Imperial voices Grand Expression Modeling + VRM 38 instrument voices 256-note polyphony Bluetooth MIDI + audio Smart Pianist app compatible Powerful 2-way speaker system (30W + 30W) 3-pedal unit with half-pedal support Best For: Serious students, advanced home players, anyone who wants the authentic acoustic piano experience without the tuning, maintenance, and space requirements. Downsides? It's around $3,200–$3,500 depending on finish. That's real money. And it's heavy. You're not moving this thing without a buddy (or two). My Take: If you're serious about piano and want something for your home that'll inspire you every time you walk past it, the CLP-835 is where the Clavinova magic really kicks in. It's the sweet spot of the entire CLP range. You get almost everything the higher models have, without the eye-watering price of the CLP-885. This piano honestly makes me forget I'm not playing an acoustic. 3. Yamaha CLP-885 — Best Premium Digital Piano 💬 "The best digital piano I've ever played. Full stop." Yamaha CLP-885 Why I Recommend It: I'm not going to sugarcoat it: the CLP-885 is expensive. Like, really expensive. But if you have the budget, this is as close to a grand piano experience as digital gets in 2026. The GrandTouch keyboard (not GrandTouch- S , the full GrandTouch) features solid wooden keys with individual counterweights and authentic escapement. Three sensors per key capture every nuance of your playing. It genuinely feels like sitting at a Yamaha grand. I'm not exaggerating. The speaker system is a beast: six speakers, diffusers, bidirectional horns, and a redesigned cabinet that projects sound both forward and backward. It fills a room the way an acoustic does. The voices include the CFX and Bösendorfer Imperial with binaural sampling, plus a collection of historical pianos and fortepianos that classical players will absolutely geek out over. And the little details: a soft-close fallboard (so you never slam the lid), a hidden touch LCD display that disappears when you're not using it, and compatibility with Yamaha's Smart Pianist app for everything from sheet music to lessons. Current Best Deal on GuitarCenter What It Has: 88 keys with GrandTouch action (wooden keys, counterweights, 3 sensors) CFX + Bösendorfer Imperial binaural voices Grand Expression Modeling + VRM 53 voices + 480 XG voices + 14 drum kits 256-note polyphony 6-speaker system with diffusers (300W total) Bluetooth MIDI + audio GP Response Damper pedal system Hidden touch LCD display Soft-close fallboard Built-in lesson library (Hanon, Czerny, Burgmüller) Best For: Advanced players, piano teachers, serious enthusiasts, and anyone who wants the absolute best digital piano experience money can buy (in an upright cabinet). Downsides? Price. You're looking at $5,000+ depending on finish (the polished ebony and white versions are even more). At that point, you could buy a decent used acoustic upright. And it weighs around 168 lbs, so... it's not going anywhere once you set it up. My Take: If you've got the budget and you want a digital piano that makes you forget it's digital, this is the one. I've played acoustic grands that don't feel this good. The CLP-885 is Yamaha saying "we dare you to tell the difference." For most people, the CLP-835 is the smarter buy. But if you want the absolute pinnacle? This is it. 4. Roland FP-90X — Best High-End Portable 💬 "The portable piano that doesn't compromise on anything." Roland FP-90X Why I Recommend It: Most portable pianos make trade-offs. Smaller speakers, simpler key action, fewer features. The FP-90X says "nah" to all of that. It has Roland's PHA-50 hybrid key action, real wood combined with molded materials. It feels premium without being ridiculously heavy. The sound engine is Roland's PureAcoustic Piano Modeling, which doesn't use samples at all. Instead, it mathematically models how every component of a piano interacts in real time. The result is a sound that's eerily organic and endlessly expressive. Current Best Deal on Amazon What It Has: 88 keys with PHA-50 hybrid action (wood + molded) PureAcoustic Piano Modeling sound engine 362 voices 256-note polyphony Bluetooth MIDI + audio Powerful 4-speaker system (60W total) Mic input with effects USB audio recording Headphone 3D ambience Best For: Advanced players who need a portable instrument that doesn't sacrifice sound or feel. Perfect for studio musicians, gigging pianists, and anyone who wants Roland's best in a slab-style form factor. Downsides? Pricy, around $2,300. And while it's technically portable, it's one of the heavier "portable" options at around 51 lbs. You'll want a quality stand because an X-stand looks ridiculous under something this premium. My Take: If you need a portable piano that can do everything and sound incredible doing it, the FP-90X is in a class of its own. It's the only portable I've played that genuinely made me forget I wasn't sitting at a console. Brand Showdown: Yamaha vs Roland vs Kawai vs Casio Yamaha, Roland, Kawai, and Casio are all reputable digital piano brands, but each leads in different areas. Yamaha is the safest all-rounder, Roland excels in key action, Kawai is known for warm piano tone, and Casio often wins on value, especially in Privia models like the PX-S1100. Yamaha. The safe choice. Incredible piano tone (they literally make acoustic grands), reliable build quality, and the most familiar name in the game. Their Clavinova line is the gold standard for home digital pianos. If you're unsure, go Yamaha. You won't regret it. Roland. The innovator. Roland doesn't make acoustic pianos. Instead, they use modeling technology rather than samples to create sound. Their PureAcoustic Modeling engine mathematically simulates how a piano works in real time, producing extremely responsive and organic tone. Their key actions are consistently excellent, even at lower price points. Best Bluetooth implementation in the business. Kawai. The pianist's brand. Kawai has been making acoustic pianos since 1927, and their digital pianos reflect that heritage. The key actions tend to be the most realistic in their respective price classes. If touch and feel are your top priorities, Kawai often wins. Casio. The value king. Casio gets unfairly overlooked because of their calculator reputation, but their Privia line is legit . They consistently deliver the slimmest, lightest designs with surprisingly good sound and feel. If space or budget is a concern, look at Casio first. Digital Piano Buyer's Guide: What Actually Matters The features that matter most in a digital piano are key action, piano sound, speaker quality, and pedal support. Prioritize 88 weighted keys with graded hammer action, at least 64-note polyphony, and a sustain pedal input; models like the Roland FP-10 and Yamaha P-145BT cover those essentials well. Key Action (Most Important!): This is the single most important spec. You want fully weighted, hammer-action keys . Period. Semi-weighted is fine for a cheap keyboard, but if you want to develop proper technique and transition to an acoustic piano someday, hammer action is non-negotiable. If you want to understand more about why this matters so much, check out our acoustic vs digital piano guide. Sound Engine: Two main approaches exist: sampling (recording actual piano sounds and playing them back) and modeling (mathematically simulating how a piano works). Both can sound amazing. Yamaha and Kawai primarily use sampling; Roland primarily uses modeling. The best models blend both. Polyphony: This is how many notes the piano can produce simultaneously. You'd think 88 keys = 88 notes max, right? Not quite. Sustain pedal, layers, and reverb all eat into polyphony. Aim for at least 128 notes . Ideally 256. Speakers: Portable pianos have small speakers. Console pianos have bigger, better-positioned speakers. If you're mostly playing at home and want to hear your piano the way it's meant to sound, a console with a proper speaker system makes a huge difference. If you're on a portable model, invest in good headphones. You'll hear details the built-in speakers can't reproduce. Connectivity: At minimum, you want USB to Host for connecting to learning apps and DAWs. Bluetooth MIDI is a fantastic bonus that lets you connect wirelessly to apps like Flowkey or Simply Piano . Bluetooth audio lets you stream music through the piano's speakers. Pedals: Sustain pedal is essential (most portable pianos include a basic one). A three-pedal unit with half-pedal support is important for classical music. Console pianos include this by default; portable models usually require a separate purchase. How I Tested These Pianos These digital pianos were evaluated by comparing key action, piano tone, speaker performance, features, and price-to-value across the same shortlist. Hands-on play feel, repeated A/B comparisons, and practical criteria such as Bluetooth, pedal options, and portability determined rankings, with brands like Yamaha, Roland, and Kawai judged on real playing experience. I want to be transparent about how I arrived at this list. I don't just read spec sheets and regurgitate marketing copy (looking at you, half the internet). I've physically sat down at every piano on this list. Here's what I focus on: Key feel first, always. I play the same pieces across all models: a Chopin Nocturne for dynamic range, some jazz chords for responsiveness, and basic scales for consistency. Sound quality through speakers AND headphones. Some pianos sound great through speakers but weird through headphones, and vice versa. Build quality. Does it feel like something that'll last 5+ years? Or does it creak when you play fortissimo? Real-world usability. Can I set it up without a manual? Can I change voices without diving through six menus? Is the pedal input sturdy? Value for money. I always ask: "Is there a cheaper piano that does 90% of what this one does?" Where to Buy (And Try Before You Buy) I always tell people: try to play a piano in person before buying it. Key action is a deeply personal thing. What feels amazing to me might feel too heavy or too light for you. Here's where you can do that in the US: Guitar Center . The biggest chain with the most floor models. You won't find every piano on this list, but they usually stock the Yamaha P-145BT, Roland FP-30X, and several Casio Privia models. Walk in, sit down, play for 20 minutes. Sweetwater . My personal favorite for online buying. Incredible customer service, no tax in most states, and they have a massive showroom in Fort Wayne, Indiana if you're anywhere near it. Their return policy is also generous. Amazon . Convenient and often has bundle deals (piano + stand + bench + pedal). Just make sure you're buying from an authorized dealer so your warranty is valid. Local piano dealers. Often the best place to try Kawai and higher-end Yamaha Clavinova models. These shops tend to carry fewer brands but know their products inside and out. Worth the drive. Pro tip: If you can't try in person, buy from a retailer with a solid return policy. Most reputable dealers give you 30–45 days to return. That's plenty of time to know if a piano is right for you. Frequently Asked Questions What is the best digital piano for beginners? The Yamaha P-145BT is my top recommendation for most beginners. It's affordable, reliable, and has weighted keys that feel like a real piano. If you can stretch your budget, the Roland FP-30X at around $695 is even better for long-term growth. Check out our dedicated best beginner pianos article for more options. Is a digital piano as good as a real piano? For most people? Yes, absolutely. Modern digital pianos with quality hammer-action keys and advanced sound engines are incredibly close to the real thing. The gap has narrowed dramatically in the last few years. That said, high-end acoustic pianos still have a certain organic quality that even the best digitals can't fully replicate. We go deeper on this in our acoustic vs digital piano comparison. How much should I spend on a digital piano? Depends on your goals. For beginners: $400–$500 gets you a solid instrument. Intermediate players: $700–$2,000 opens up significantly better key actions and sounds. Serious players: $2,000–$4,000 gets you a premium console that rivals acoustics. My rule of thumb: spend slightly more than you initially planned. You'll thank yourself later. What's the difference between a keyboard and a digital piano? A keyboard typically has unweighted keys, built-in speakers, and lots of sounds/rhythms. A digital piano focuses on replicating the acoustic piano experience with fully weighted keys, realistic sound, and (usually) 88 keys. If you want to learn piano , get a digital piano. If you want to mess around with sounds, a keyboard is fine. Do digital pianos need tuning? Nope. One of the biggest advantages of going digital. No tuning, no maintenance, no worrying about humidity or temperature. Just play. Are weighted keys really that important? Yes. 100%. Weighted keys build proper finger strength and technique. If you practice on unweighted keys, your fingers won't develop the control needed to play an acoustic piano well. It's like training for a marathon in slippers. How long do digital pianos last? A quality digital piano from Yamaha, Roland, Kawai, or Casio will easily last 10–20 years with normal use. The electronics rarely fail. The key actions are built to withstand millions of presses. The only thing that might feel "dated" after a decade is the sound technology, but even then, most people won't notice. Can I learn piano on a digital piano? Absolutely. In fact, digital pianos are better for learning in many ways. You can practice with headphones at any hour, connect to learning apps , record yourself, and adjust tempo with the metronome. Most piano teachers are perfectly happy with students practicing on a quality digital piano. Still Not Sure? Here's My TL;DR: On a tight budget? Yamaha P-145BT, Roland FP-10, or Kawai ES60. The P-145BT is the safest all-rounder; the FP-10 has the best key feel; the ES60 has the best sound. Ready to invest a bit more? Roland FP-30X at ~$695. It's the best value portable piano right now and you won't need to upgrade for years. Want a home piano that looks and sounds like the real deal? Yamaha CLP-835. This is where "digital" starts to feel like "acoustic." Money is no object? Yamaha CLP-885. I've played grand pianos that don't feel this good. Need portability + power? Kawai ES920 (~$1,950) or Roland FP-90X (~$2,300), depending on whether you prefer sampling (Kawai) or modeling (Roland). Here's the real secret though: any piano on this list is a solid choice. The worst thing you can do is spend six months researching and zero months playing. Pick one in your budget, sit down, and start making music. And if you're just getting started on your piano journey, check out our guide to the best online piano lessons and our breakdown of how to teach yourself piano . The instrument is only half the equation. The other half is how you learn. Now go play something. 🎹 We are a participant in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program, an affiliate advertising program designed to provide a means for us to earn fees by linking to Amazon.com and affiliated sites.

author: Katarina
h1: Stephen Ridley's Piano Academy: The Disturbing Truth
headings: Protect Your Wallet, Not the Con Artist
text: A crimson-robed man bangs out pop songs on his piano while proclaiming, "Doesn't that sound amazing?" So begins the siren call of Stephen Ridley's piano course ads, which pop up across YouTube and beyond. He tantalizes viewers with the idea that for just $1,400 , his "revolutionary" Ridley method can transform tone-deaf amateurs into virtuoso pianists able to dazzle any audience. But an investigation into Ridley's inflated credentials and high-pressure sales tactics indicates his Piano Masterclass is little more than a scam to extract money from unwitting students on behalf of the controversial Church of Scientology. TL;DR Is it revolutionary? Hell no. Does it work? Barely. Is it worth $1,400? Absolutely not. If you’re a total beginner chasing quick pop wins, Ridley’s hype might hook you for a hot second, but bail before the bill hits. If you want real piano chops without the culty cash grab, hunt down something legit. Whatever you do, don’t buy the robed wizard act. True mastery demands sweat, not slick sales funnels. And no "method" can shortcut the grind. The Fabricated Musical Prodigy "I studied at some of the best music schools in the world, including the Royal College of Music in London and the Juilliard School in New York," boasts Ridley. Yet nowhere in his official biography does it state he actually attended or graduated from these elite institutions. It instead says he worked in investment banking before becoming a musician. This seeming embellishment of his educational background raises immediate red flags. Stephen Ridley's bio and ads also claim he's played with music legends like Stevie Wonder . But besides his own assertions, there exists no evidence of him ever performing with Wonder or other stars he name-drops. Reviews from actual musicians characterize his piano skills as mediocre at best, akin to a "child who just learned about chords." Hardly the awe-inspiring prowess expected from a world-class, Julliard-polished prodigy. So how did this apparently average pianist suddenly develop a "revolutionary" method for playing piano after a career in high finance? That brings us to his so-called breakthrough. Debunking the "Ridley Method" In his pontificating piano course ads, Ridley introduces viewers to his " Ridley Method " which he claims allows students to play an endless array of songs using just four simple chords. The Ridley Piano Method claims that it is an accelerated learning approach designed to help students play confidently up to 10 times faster than traditional methods. Ideal for beginners and those with little to no musical experience, this piano method simplifies piano learning by breaking it down into 55 easy-to-follow steps. "Students" seen giving miraculous testimonials in the ads gush about how they can suddenly sit down and perform any pop song that comes on the radio. But as scores of professional and hobbyist musicians have repeatedly pointed out online, these four chords constitute one of the most common and beginner-friendly chord progressions in pop music. An Australian comedy band called The Axis of Awesome went viral over a decade ago for their humorous song " Four Chord Song ," which showed how the simplistic chord sequence showed up in dozens of popular hits. Many music teachers state they teach students those exact four chords in the very first lessons. Yet Ridley presents this rudimentary chord progression as his own proprietary secret sauce - the backbone of the "Ridley Method." This seems to imply taking credit for "discovering" a basic musical concept as universal as the color blue. Actual musicians allege he relies on flashy marketing and dramatic persona to disguise this lack of originality or substance. Empty Promises and Upsells The grandiose claims don't stop with taking ownership of Education 101 piano chords. Ridley also asserts that students who enroll in his $1,400 online piano course can "play beautifully after just a few lessons" and reach performance "Level 10" within months. But personal reviews expose this as well to be massaged marketing hype: "The lessons are too short and then instructed to go learn on your own and will be easy and fast- neither are true...I practiced for 1⁄2 to 1 hour and other than finger drills and struggling to memorize scales- it doesn’t deliver." Such first-hand accounts characterize Ridley's course as less of a structured educational program and more of an eclectic grab-bag of incomplete independent exercises. You apparently get left to teach yourself despite little prior foundation. Again Ridley seems to vastly overstate the value and efficacy of his slapdash product. He also refuses to allow interested buyers to just purchase his lesson videos alone. You must commit to the entire $1,400 package, which student reviews imply contains lots of recycled self-helpy padding outside the actual piano content. Ridley further stonewalls requests about payment plans, forcing people to shell out the lump sum or walk away. Capping off the entire high-pressure sales bonanza is the so-called "free" eBook Ridley promises webinar viewers for sitting through the hours-long infomercials for his course. But this "Christmas gift" turns out to be a meager 26 pages of rehashed information from the webinar. Just one more carrot dangled to lure students into his overpriced program. Funneling Funds to Scientology If Ridley brazenly misrepresents his skills and the nature of his product, where does all the money from his piano course actually go? Potentially straight into the coffers of the controversial Church of Scientology. Online sleuths discovered that Ridley resides near the international headquarters for Scientology. His self-helpy, feel-good rhetoric also closely resembles the manipulation tactics for which Scientology receives widespread criticism. Phrases like "revolutionize your life" and "achieve your dreams" permeate his sales pitches. Moreover, the structured levels for advancing piano skill in his course strongly mirror Scientology's own tiered system for spiritual enlightenment, which requires members to keep paying more and more to climb the rungs. The financial parallels seem too conspicuous to ignore. While no concrete paper trail of Ridley's payments to Scientology exists yet, the body of circumstantial evidence continues mounting. His alleged lack of transparency regarding the true nature of his offerings combined with his close geographic and ideological ties to a controversial religious institution leave his motives in question. Protect Your Wallet, Not the Con Artist Stephen Ridley ultimately acts as a sort of pianistic Wizard of Oz - big, loud, and commanding attention from behind a curtain of smoke and mirrors. Strip away the dramatic costumery, the lighting and camera angles, the scripted dialogue, and precious little musical knowledge remains. What does continue unchecked is his extensive media campaign to separate thousands of students from their hard-earned money. The individual consumer must decide for themselves whether Ridley's course offers any legitimate value under all the convoluted theatrics. But they would be wise to balance his self-styled rags-to-riches story ripe for the movies with the simpler tales of misgiving from ordinary people regretting their purchases. In the meantime, legitimate online courses and teachers still provide earnest students the opportunity to develop their talents sans scams. Because as much as Stephen Ridley may bang the keys while making baffling appeals to join his expensive program, perhaps the simplest advice is not to let the wolf in, in the first place. Especially one in strange robes with undisclosed ties to groups exhibiting cultish behaviors and insatiable greed.

og_title: How to Learn Piano by Yourself: A Step-by-Step Guide
og_desc: Teach yourself piano with a keyboard, one course, and 30 minutes a day. The order to learn things in, how to practice, and how to catch your own mistakes.
author: Katarina
h1: How to learn piano by yourself: A Step-by-Step Guide
headings: Step 1: Get to Know the Instrument
Step 2: Learn Enough Theory to Read
text: You can teach yourself piano. A keyboard, one course you stick with, and thirty focused minutes a day will have you playing songs people recognize inside of a few months. The catch is that nobody corrects your fingering, and nobody tells you that you have been drilling the same mistake for three weeks. This guide covers what to learn, in what order, and how to catch your own errors along the way. TL;DR Self-teaching works. Online courses and apps like Pianoforall and Simply Piano supply the structure a teacher would. Start with the boring parts. Key layout, posture, hand position, and enough theory to read a staff. Practice with a target. One goal per session, a metronome running, and a recording you listen back to. Use the tech. Apps, video tutorials, and structured courses close the feedback gap. Plan for the slumps. Book a performance, even a small one, and find other learners to answer your questions. Climb in order. Five-finger exercises, then scales and chords, then pieces, then the genre you sat down for in the first place. Three habits carry you: play under tempo, isolate the bars you keep flubbing, and show up on the days you don't feel like it. What's coming: AI feedback tools and VR lessons will sharpen the practice loop. Your reason for sitting down at the keys stays yours. More People Are Teaching Themselves The pandemic years pushed a lot of people toward instruments they had never touched. Piano sales climbed, and online learning platforms signed up beginners faster than they could build lessons for them. Source: Technavio "We've seen a 300% increase in new users since March 2020," says Sarah Chen, CEO of an online piano learning platform. "People are realizing that they don't need to commit to expensive, time-consuming lessons to enjoy playing an instrument." The same shift hit coding, languages, and cooking. Piano sits at the harder end of that list, because bad technique compounds and few beginners hear their own timing drift. Self-teaching still works for people who build the structure a teacher would have handed them. The Myth of the "Natural" Musician Teachers used to sort students into the gifted and the rest, and the rest believed them. Anders Ericsson spent a career dismantling that idea. "The idea that expert performance reflects basic abilities that cannot be changed by training is not scientifically defensible," he wrote in Peak: Secrets from the New Science of Expertise. What separates the strong players from the stuck ones is the quality of their practice: what they work on, how they correct it, how fast they hear whether it worked. You control the first two on your own. The third you have to build, with recordings, a metronome, and an app that tells you when you missed the note. Build the Foundation Beginners who skip the foundations spend their second year unlearning their first. Music theory 101. Read a staff, count a time signature, recognize a key signature. Musictheory.net teaches all of it free, with drills. Posture and hand shape. Bench height, wrist level, shoulders down. Watch a channel like Piano TV and copy the frame, not the notes. Finger exercises. The Hanon exercises have built dexterity for pianists since the 1870s and cost nothing online. Ten minutes a session is plenty. Apps and Online Courses A phone app can hear your notes and flag the wrong ones. That is the piece self-teaching used to be missing, and it is the reason a beginner in 2026 progresses faster than one in 2006. Pianoforall takes an order-of-operations approach that suits self-teachers: rhythm-style piano and recognizable songs first, classical technique and sight-reading after. You get something worth playing for a friend in week two, which is what keeps most people at the bench long enough to reach the harder material. " What sets Pianoforall apart is its emphasis on practical skills, " notes Dr. Elena R., a music education researcher at Berklee College of Music. "By teaching students to play recognizable tunes early on, it taps into the intrinsic motivation that's so crucial for sustained learning." The course runs 300+ video lessons across 10 interactive e-books . You set the pace and go back over the chapters that beat you. Other platforms worth comparing: Flowkey : listens as you play and corrects you in real time Simply Piano : gamified, strong on daily streaks Playground Sessions : co-created by Quincy Jones, heavy on pop repertoire Most self-taught pianists end up running two of these at once, one for structure and one for songs. Practice That Works Twenty minutes with a target beats an hour of noodling. Name the goal before you sit down. "Get better at piano" gives you nothing to check. "Play the G major scale, hands together, at 80 bpm by Friday" tells you when you're done. Run the metronome. Your internal clock speeds up on the easy bars and drags on the hard ones. You will not hear it without the click. Record yourself once a week. Your phone is fine. Playback catches the mistakes your hands hide from your ears. Play under tempo. Half speed builds the right movement. Full speed at week one builds the wrong movement and locks it in. Drill the four bars that keep breaking. Running a piece top to bottom rehearses the parts you already own and skims the part you don't. Problems You'll Hit The plateau. Progress stalls after the first quick wins. Change what you practice, not how long you practice. The motivation dip. No teacher waits for you on Tuesday, so nothing happens when you skip. Book a low-stakes performance for family or post a progress video, and give yourself a date. Bad habits. Collapsed wrists and flat fingers creep in when nobody watches. Film your hands from the side once a month and compare the frame against a tutorial. Picking the wrong pieces. A piece three levels above you costs a month and teaches you little. Post your video in a forum and ask what to learn next. Find Other Learners "Self-taught" describes the lesson plan. The people who stay with it collect a few others who play. "The self-taught community has been invaluable," says Michael Chang, a software engineer who started learning piano during the pandemic. "Sharing progress videos on Instagram and getting feedback from other learners has kept me accountable and inspired." A forum thread, a Discord server, or two friends who also practice will answer questions a search engine can't and will notice when you go quiet for a month. The Step-by-Step Guide Work through these in order. Each step assumes the one before it. Step 1: Get to Know the Instrument Read the keyboard: A full-sized piano has 88 keys. The pattern repeats every 12 keys: 7 white, 5 black. White keys are the naturals, A through G. Black keys are the sharps and flats. Set your posture: Sit at the middle of the keyboard. Back straight, shoulders loose. Feet flat on the floor or a footrest. Elbows level with the keys. Shape your hands: Curve your fingers as if you're holding a ball. Keep your wrists level with your hands, neither dropped nor raised. Step 2: Learn Enough Theory to Read The musical alphabet: Seven note names, A through G. The pattern repeats up and down the keyboard. Octaves: An octave spans one pitch to the pitch at double or half its frequency. Time signatures: Start with 4/4, 3/4, and 2/4. Learn what the top and bottom numbers each control. Key signatures: Tell major from minor by ear and on the page. Track which sharps and flats a key carries. Musictheory.net covers all four with free interactive drills. Step 3: Start with Simple Exercises Five-finger exercises: Play C, D, E, F, G with your right hand. Repeat with your left. Scales: C major first. One hand at a time, then both together. Chord progressions: Learn C, F, and G. Drill the changes between them until your hand stops looking. Step 4: Read Sheet Music The staff: Treble clef and bass clef. Memorize the notes on every line and space. Note values: Whole, half, quarter, eighth. Tie each one to a count you can tap. Sight-reading: Open with pieces below your playing level. Raise the difficulty a notch at a time. Step 5: Build Your Rhythm Use a metronome: Set a slow tempo and add a few bpm each session. Keep time on exercises you already know before you add a new piece. Learn the common feels: A waltz in 3/4 and a march in 4/4 sit under most of what you'll play. Clap before you play: Clap a new piece's rhythm through once. Your hands learn the timing before they learn the notes. Step 6: Learn Your First Songs Pick a melody you know cold: "Twinkle Twinkle Little Star" and "Happy Birthday" both work. Split the hands: Right hand first, then left. Put them together once each hand runs clean on its own. Move up: Add a piece with a chord change or a new key each time one gets easy. Step 7: Explore Different Genres Classical: Bach's Minuet in G or a Mozart minuet will stretch you without breaking you. Pop: Find simplified arrangements of songs you already sing along to. Jazz and blues: Learn a blues scale and a 12-bar progression, then improvise over it. Step 8: Sharpen Your Technique Arpeggios: Start with C, F, and G major, one octave, and add speed once they're even. Dynamics: Practice a phrase at piano, then at forte. Move between them without a jump in the middle. Finger independence: Drill exercises where one finger moves while the others hold their keys down. Step 9: Set a Practice Routine Sample daily practice schedule Pick your slot: Fifteen to thirty minutes, same time each day, beats two hours on Sunday. Structure the session: Warm up on scales and exercises. Spend the bulk on one piece or one technique. Close with something you enjoy playing. Use the three techniques that pay off: Slow practice: take the hard section under tempo and raise it a few clicks at a time. Hands apart: each hand alone before the two together. Chunking: break the piece into four-bar sections and own each one. Step 10: Record and Review Film your sessions: One recording a week is enough to see the trend. Listen for the specific problem: Find the bars that drag, the notes that fall out of the chord, the dynamics that flatten. Note what improved since last month, then move on. Reset the goal: Each recording tells you what to work on next. Write it down before you close the app. Step 11: Add Outside Help Structured tutorials: A self-paced course like Pianoforall keeps your progression in order. Online communities: A pianist forum or Discord answers the questions a course doesn't cover. A few real lessons: Two or three sessions with a teacher will catch technique problems you can't see in your own footage. Book them once you have something to play. Learning piano is a long project with no finish line. Be patient with your hands and notice what you can do this month that you couldn't last month. Happy playing. Where Piano Teaching Goes Next VR lessons, AI feedback that grades your evenness bar by bar, and courses that reroute themselves around your weak spots are all close. Each one narrows the gap between practicing alone and practicing with a teacher in the room. Dr. Elena R. draws the line at the machine's edge. "While these tools are incredibly powerful, they can't replace the emotional connection and creativity that comes from making music. The goal should always be to use technology as a means to express oneself through the instrument." Conclusion Teaching yourself piano changes what you notice in music you've heard a hundred times. Take a structured course like Pianoforall , build your own curriculum from free resources, or mix self-study with a lesson every few months. Any of the three works if you keep showing up. Thelonious Monk said the piano ain't got no wrong notes. Sit down at the keys and find out what he meant.

desc: Skoove costs $12.49/month on the annual plan and has a free tier. It nails notes and timing, and ignores everything else. Who it suits, and where it stops.
og_title: Skoove Review (2026): Is This Piano Learning App Effective?
og_desc: It gets a beginner from nothing to playing a real song. It also cannot hear how long you held a note, or what your hands are doing. The honest limits, and the 2026 prices.
author: Katarina
h1: Skoove Review 2026: Honest Verdict After Testing the App
headings: What the feedback can hear, and what it can't
Does Skoove work with a MIDI keyboard?
Does Skoove work with an acoustic piano?
Can Skoove replace a piano teacher?
Is Skoove good for advanced players?
How many lessons does Skoove have?

text: Skoove is a piano learning app that listens while you play and tells you whether you hit the right notes. It costs €12.49 a month on the annual plan (€149.99 up front), it has a free tier that never expires, and it is one of the better ways for an adult beginner to get from nothing to playing recognizable songs. It also stops earlier than its marketing suggests. The feedback engine checks pitch and timing, and it does that well. It cannot hear how long you hold a note, how tense your hand is, or whether your fingering will still work three bars later. That gap sets the ceiling on what Skoove can teach you, and it arrives around the point most people call intermediate. Buy it if you're starting from zero and want structure. Skip it if you already play and want to get better at playing rather than at learning songs. Skoove review scores Last checked September 2026 Overall rating 7/10 Editor’s score Getting started 9/10 The strongest thing it does. Zero to a recognizable song without a teacher. Feedback quality 7/10 Near-perfect on pitch and timing, blind to duration, tone and hand shape. How far it goes 5/10 Plateaus in early intermediate. The Advanced courses are not advanced. Value 7/10 The free tier and the annual price are fair. You are renting, not owning. Scored as a self-guided learning app for adult beginners, which is the job it is built for. What Skoove costs in 2026 Plan Price Notes Free (Skoove Basic) €0 Selected lessons from each course, no card required, no time limit 1 month €29.99/month Billed monthly 3 months €19.99/month €59.99 charged quarterly 12 months €12.49/month €149.99 charged up front, includes a 7-day free trial Lifetime Not published One-time payment, arranged by emailing Skoove support Prices shown are from Skoove's own pricing page and appear in your local currency; US readers see the same numbers in dollars, so the annual plan lands at about $149.99. Two things worth knowing before you enter a card. The 7-day trial converts to a paid year unless you cancel inside the week. And Skoove's published terms say cancelling stops future renewals but gives no partial refund for time you haven't used, so the free tier is a safer way to look around than the trial is. How Skoove works Every lesson runs the same three steps. You listen to the passage, you learn it in slow segments with the notes lighting up on an on-screen keyboard and on the sheet music, then you play it while the app follows along. The app tracks what you play through one of three inputs: USB MIDI , using a USB-to-Host cable from a digital piano Bluetooth MIDI , for keyboards that support it Your device's microphone , which works with any instrument including an acoustic piano The microphone option is why Skoove works for people with an upright in the hall and no digital keyboard, and it's a real advantage over apps that need MIDI. It's also the weaker input. Skoove's own help pages recommend a quiet room and note that background noise confuses the note detection, so if you own a digital piano, connect it by cable and stop thinking about it. Skoove advertises over 1,000 lessons and songs across pop, rock, jazz, blues, and classical, and says it has more than 3 million learners. Premium includes one-to-one messaging with its music instructors, which is a better feature than it sounds: it means a human answers when you get stuck on something the app can't explain. What the feedback can hear, and what it can't This is the part of Skoove that decides whether it suits you, and most reviews skip it. The note detection does its job well. Play the right notes at the right moment and Skoove knows. One independent reviewer who tested it at length called the detection "virtually perfect" for beginner material, and that matches what the app is built to do. Skoove grades pitch and timing, and stops there. It does not grade duration, so a passage of half notes played as short stabs still scores full marks as long as each note starts in the right place. It cannot hear phrasing, dynamics beyond the crudest level, pedalling, or tone. It has no idea what your hands are doing, so collapsed wrists, flat fingers, and a thumb tucked under at the wrong moment all pass unnoticed. Skoove checks Skoove cannot check Whether you played the right note How long you held it Whether you played it on the beat Whether the phrase breathes Whether you kept up with the track Your hand shape, wrist height, or fingering Whether you finished the lesson Your pedalling and tone For a beginner, none of this matters much. Right notes, right time is the whole job in month one, and getting instant confirmation is worth more than any other feature in the app. For anyone past that, the missing half is the half that separates playing notes from playing music. That is the honest case for adding a teacher later, or at least filming your hands, rather than the case against Skoove. Where the curriculum stops Skoove's courses run from Kids and Beginner through to Advanced. The labels overstate the top end. Independent testing found that many lessons filed under Advanced sit closer to intermediate, and that the progression thins out once you're past early intermediate material. Reviewers who went looking for a technical framework, meaning hand independence, chord inversions, and fingering through awkward passages, found it missing. You can finish a lot of Skoove and know the notes to many songs without having built the mechanics underneath them. Music theory gets similar treatment. It's woven into the song lessons rather than taught as a subject, which keeps beginners moving but leaves gaps. If you want to understand why a progression works, read a lead sheet, or improvise, Skoove is not the tool. None of this makes it a bad app. It makes it a beginner's app with an intermediate ceiling, priced and marketed as though the ceiling weren't there. Who Skoove is for Good fit: Adult beginners who want structure and can't face a metronome and a method book Anyone with an acoustic piano and no MIDI keyboard, since microphone input works Learners who need a reason to sit down, and who respond to songs they recognize Parents looking for an ad-free app a child can use without supervision Poor fit: Intermediate players who already read music and want technique Anyone whose goal is improvisation, theory, or playing by ear Learners chasing exam grades or classical repertoire at any depth Anyone who wants to own their materials rather than rent access How Skoove compares Platform Feedback Strongest at Payment Skoove MIDI or microphone, pitch and timing Getting a complete beginner reading and playing Subscription Flowkey MIDI or microphone A larger song library, similar ceiling Subscription Simply Piano MIDI or microphone, gamified Keeping children and streak-driven adults at it Subscription Playground Sessions MIDI, more detailed scoring Deeper progression for intermediates Subscription Pianoforall None, it's a course not an app Chords, styles, and playing by ear One-time We've tested these against each other in our guide to the best online piano lessons , which is the place to start if you haven't settled on a platform. The case for Pianoforall instead Pianoforall solves a different problem, and for some readers it's the better purchase. It's a course rather than an app: around 25 hours of video embedded in ten e-books, bought once with no subscription. It teaches chord patterns and rhythm styles first, so you're playing something that sounds like music within weeks, and it spends real time on playing by ear and improvising. Those are the two things Skoove leaves out. You give up the feedback loop. Nothing listens to you, nothing tells you that bar 12 was wrong, and nobody chases you when you skip a week. That suits a self-directed learner and frustrates everyone else. The honest split: pick Skoove if you need the app to keep you honest, and Pianoforall if you'd rather own the material and work at your own pace. Frequently asked questions How much does Skoove cost? Skoove Premium costs €29.99 a month billed monthly, €19.99 a month billed quarterly (€59.99 every three months), or €12.49 a month billed yearly (€149.99 charged up front). US pricing mirrors these figures in dollars. A free tier with selected lessons is available with no card and no time limit. Is Skoove free? There's a free tier called Skoove Basic, with no time limit, that gives you selected lessons from each course with no credit card required. Premium adds the full library, and its 7-day trial does ask for payment details and converts to a paid plan unless you cancel first. Does Skoove work with a MIDI keyboard? Yes. Skoove connects over USB MIDI using a USB-to-Host cable, over Bluetooth MIDI on keyboards that support it, or through your device's microphone. If you have a digital piano, use a cable, because microphone detection struggles with background noise. Does Skoove work with an acoustic piano? Yes, through your device's microphone. This is one of Skoove's genuine advantages over apps that require a MIDI connection. Play in a quiet room, since noise interferes with note detection. Can Skoove replace a piano teacher? No. Skoove checks whether you played the right notes at the right time. It cannot see your hands, so it misses tension, hand shape, and fingering, and it doesn't grade note length, phrasing, or pedalling. It works well alongside occasional lessons rather than instead of them. Is Skoove good for advanced players? No. Independent testing found that much of Skoove's Advanced material sits closer to intermediate and that the progression thins out past early intermediate. Advanced players will exhaust it in weeks. How many lessons does Skoove have? Skoove advertises over 1,000 lessons and songs across pop, rock, jazz, blues, and classical, organised into courses from Kids and Beginner through Advanced, and the library keeps growing. Does Skoove teach music theory? Lightly. Theory is folded into song lessons rather than taught as a subject, which suits beginners but leaves gaps. Skoove won't teach you to read a lead sheet, understand harmony, or improvise. Can I get a refund from Skoove? Skoove's published terms say you can cancel at any time, that access continues to the end of the billing period, and that no partial refunds are given for unused time. Use the free tier to evaluate it rather than relying on getting money back. Is Skoove worth it? For an adult beginner who wants structure and instant feedback, yes, and the annual plan is where the value sits. For an intermediate player wanting technique, theory, or improvisation, the money is better spent on lessons or on a course like Pianoforall. The verdict Skoove does the hardest part of learning piano well: it gets a beginner from nothing to playing a song they recognize, and it confirms in real time that they're getting it right. The microphone option means an acoustic piano is no obstacle, the free tier lets you check the fit without a card, and the annual price is less than one in-person lesson a month. Its limits are real and worth naming. It hears pitch and timing, and nothing else that matters. Its advanced material isn't advanced. Its theory is thin. Start on the free tier. If the method suits you, the annual plan is good value for the first year or two of playing. Plan on outgrowing it, and treat that as the app doing its job rather than failing at one.

text: The Loog Piano is a $249, 37-key digital piano built for children aged 3 to 8. It sounds good, it survives a playroom, and the app and flashcards get a young child playing in an afternoon. Its keys are 21% narrower than a real piano's, which is the fact that decides whether you should buy one. Buy it for a small child who needs a first instrument they'll enjoy. Skip it for an adult beginner, for a teenager, or for any child who already takes lessons. Those buyers want full-size keys, and a 61-key keyboard in the same price range gives them that. Loog Piano review scores Last checked September 2026 Overall rating 7/10 Editor’s score Fun factor 9/10 A three-year-old can switch it on and play something alone. Actual learning 6/10 Narrow keys and three octaves cap what transfers to a real piano. Ease of use 8/10 One knob, one sound, no menus. Value 7/10 Fair for what it is. A 61-key rival buys more instrument. Scored as a first instrument for a young child, which is what Loog built it to be. Specifications Price $249 (list $299) Keys 37 (3 octaves), velocity sensitive Key width 0.73 in / 18.5 mm white keys Key material ABS plastic Action Synth action, not weighted Sounds One piano voice Speakers Built-in stereo Battery 3000 mAh, up to 8 hours Connectivity USB-C (MIDI and charging), MIDI over Bluetooth Jacks 3.5 mm headphones, sustain pedal, octave shifter Size 18.92 × 7.5 × 2.71 in (480.8 × 190.5 × 68.9 mm) Weight 3.64 lb (1.65 kg) Materials Solid wood side panels, polyester fabric top In the box Piano, chord and scale flashcards, printed guide, USB-C cable Age range Manufacturer says 3 and up The key width is the whole review Loog's white keys measure 18.5 mm across. An acoustic piano's measure about 23.5 mm. Every review of this instrument should lead with that number, and almost none of them mention it. The difference compounds across the keyboard: Loog Piano Standard piano White key width 18.5 mm 23.5 mm One octave (7 white keys) 129.5 mm 164.5 mm Full keyboard span 480 mm (37 keys) about 1,225 mm (88 keys) A child who can stretch an octave on a Loog has to reach 27% further to do the same thing on a real piano. Hand span is the limit that decides when a young player can start playing octaves and full chords, so a narrow keyboard changes what they're learning. The notes transfer. The distances don't. For a five-year-old, that trade is worth making. Their hands can't span a standard octave anyway, and narrow keys let them play chord shapes years earlier than they otherwise could. For a nine-year-old, or anyone older, it works against them: they build muscle memory at one scale and have to rebuild it at another. That single fact explains the review scores below. Fun: high. Actual learning: middling. Sound and playing feel Loog made an unusual choice for a kids' keyboard: one piano sound, and no drum kits, no strings, no demo songs. A child who sits down can only make piano noises, which keeps the instrument pointed at learning rather than at button-pressing. Loog’s own demo, played by Luciano Supervielle. The sound itself is good for the size. The stereo speakers fill a bedroom, and the velocity-sensitive keys respond to how hard they're struck, so a child hears the difference between soft and loud from the first session. That responsiveness matters more for early learning than most spec-sheet features, because dynamics are where playing starts to feel like music. The action is synth-style rather than weighted, which is standard at this price and this size. The keys are ABS plastic with a 9 mm keyboard depth. One independent reviewer who bought a unit called the plastic "pretty atrocious" and the keys "almost unplayably cramped" for adult hands. Adult hands are not the target, and that assessment lines up with the key width: this is a child's instrument, and it feels like one under a grown-up's fingers. The app, the flashcards, and the Duolingo version The Loog Piano app has now launched. It runs video lessons, a chord section, game-style exercises, and play-along songs, and it connects to the piano over Bluetooth MIDI so it can hear what's being played and respond. The flashcards in the box cover chords and scales with no screen involved, which is the part parents tend to appreciate most. Alternating between cards and app keeps a young child's attention longer than either does alone. There's also a Loog x Duolingo Piano , same $249, which swaps the standard flashcards for Duolingo-branded ones and adds a wooden phone stand. It's built to pair with Duolingo's music course, which teaches sight reading and ear training and licenses more than 60 recordings from Sony Music, including tracks by Whitney Houston, Hozier, and Pharrell Williams. Picking between them comes down to whether your child already uses Duolingo. The hardware is the same. What 37 keys can and can't do Three octaves covers most beginner repertoire and almost all single-line melodies. The octave shifter accessory moves the range up or down, which extends what's reachable without adding keys. It can't handle two-handed playing with any spread. Classical writing puts the left hand two octaves below the right as a matter of course, and on 37 keys the hands run into each other. A child will hit this ceiling around the time they start playing pieces with a real bass line, which for a motivated learner is somewhere in year one or two. Plan on this being an instrument they outgrow rather than one they keep. Build quality, and the Kickstarter history The wood side panels and fabric top look better than anything else at this price, and the single volume knob means a three-year-old can operate it alone. The design has won recognition, including a 2024 Good Design Award from the Chicago Athenaeum Museum of Architecture and Design. The original Kickstarter pitch. Useful context for the delivery history below. The launch was rough, and buyers should know it. The Loog Piano shipped through Kickstarter more than six months behind schedule, with specifications that changed during the campaign. At least one reviewer received a unit that wouldn't power on, and reported that the volume potentiometer is soldered to the board without support, and that fitting the optional legs means removing the rubber feet for good. Retail units have been shipping for a while now and those complaints have faded from recent feedback. Buy from a seller with a clean return process anyway, and test everything in the first week. How it compares Instrument Keys Key width Action Best for Loog Piano 37 Narrow (18.5 mm) Synth, velocity sensitive Children 3-8, first instrument Casio Casiotone CT-S1 61 Full size Synth with a semi-weighted feel A first keyboard that lasts past year two Yamaha Piaggero NP-12 61 Full size Piano-style, touch sensitive Learners heading toward real repertoire Any 88-key weighted digital 88 Full size Hammer action Anyone serious about learning piano Prices move, so check our guide to the best beginner pianos for what these cost now. The short version: for the price of a Loog, an adult beginner can buy a 61-key instrument with full-size keys, and they should. Who should buy the Loog Piano Buy it if: Your child is between about 3 and 8 and has never played anything You want an instrument that looks good enough to leave out in the living room Screen-free practice matters to you, and the flashcards appeal You want a real instrument rather than a toy keyboard, at toy-keyboard scale Skip it if: You're an adult beginner, whatever the marketing says Your child is nine or older, or already takes lessons You want one instrument that lasts years rather than one that gets outgrown You need more than a piano sound Frequently asked questions How much does the Loog Piano cost? The Loog Piano costs $249, down from a $299 list price. The Loog x Duolingo Piano is the same $249 and includes Duolingo flashcards and a wooden phone stand instead of the standard accessories. Bundles with a stand, case, or legs cost extra and come and go from stock. Are the Loog Piano keys full size? No. Loog's white keys are 0.73 inches (18.5 mm) wide, against about 0.93 inches (23.5 mm) on a standard piano, which makes them 21% narrower. That suits small hands and is the main reason the instrument suits young children rather than adults. Is the Loog Piano good for adult beginners? No. The keys are too narrow and too few for adult hands, and one reviewer described them as almost unplayably cramped. An adult beginner gets far more from a 61-key keyboard with full-size keys at a similar price. How many keys does the Loog Piano have? 37 keys, which is three octaves. That covers most beginner melodies, and the optional octave shifter moves the range up or down. It runs out when a piece needs the hands spread far apart. Are the Loog Piano keys weighted? No. They are synth-action and velocity sensitive, so they respond to how hard you play but have no hammer weight. Weighted actions start on larger, heavier instruments. Does the Loog Piano need the app? No. The flashcards in the box teach chords and scales with no screen. The app adds video lessons, exercises, and play-along songs, and connects over Bluetooth MIDI so it can respond to what your child plays. What age is the Loog Piano for? Loog says 3 and up. In practice it fits children from about 3 to 8. Past that, hands grow into full-size keys and three octaves starts to limit what they can play. Can you connect the Loog Piano to a computer? Yes. It sends MIDI over USB-C and over Bluetooth, so it works as a controller for any music software. It also takes a sustain pedal and has a 3.5 mm headphone jack for silent practice. How long does the Loog Piano battery last? Up to 8 hours from its 3000 mAh battery, charged over USB-C. That is enough for several weeks of a young child's practice between charges. Is the Loog Piano worth it? For a child aged 3 to 8, yes. You are paying a premium over a plastic keyboard for real wood, a good piano sound, velocity-sensitive keys, and a learning system that works. For anyone older, the same money buys a more useful instrument elsewhere. The verdict The Loog Piano is the nicest first instrument you can put in front of a small child, and it is the wrong purchase for everyone else. Loog built it for short fingers and short attention spans, and on those terms it succeeds: it looks good, it sounds good, it survives being left out, and children play it without being asked. The narrow keys buy that success and set the limit on it. A young child gains years of playing they couldn't otherwise have. An older one starts building habits at the wrong scale. If your child is three and curious, this is money well spent. If your child is nine, or the beginner is you, spend it on something with full-size keys .
